Author Interview: Joy Harjo on Poetry & Picture Books
opened.information:
Source: https://cynthialeitichsmith.com/2023/03/author-interview-joy-harjo-remember/
Title: Author Interview: Joy Harjo on Poetry & Picture Books
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
By AJ Eversole
Today on Cynsations I am thrilled to present an interview with former, U.S. Poet Laureate, Joy Harjo. Her latest picture book, _Remember_ (Random House Studio, 2023) released last week. Illustrated by Caldecott Medalist Michaela Goade,_Remember_, is a poem in picture book form.
**What is the heart of _Remember_?**
I used to ask this of my creative writing students when I taught. The heart of this poem can be found by the rhythm, the beat that runs through and is repeated in the word “Remember.” It pumps life in the poem. The driving force reminds us that are all connected and ultimately we are earth or Ekvnvcvke.
**What do you think of children as an audience for poetry?**
Children can be natural poets in that they naturally play with whatever materials are at hand. Word play is a given. They like ear surprises, respond to rhythm and music. They love poetry and when given a change to make their own poems are usually eager to participate.
**Do children as an audience change the way you package or present a poem?**
I think this depends on the age and the poem. I did not write the poem “Remember” specifically for children. The poem was in response to a request to write a poem to advise younger up-and-coming poets, when I was but a younger and up-and-coming poet myself. I wrote the poem in the seventies. It was published in my first book She Had Some Horses (W. W. Norton) which was published in 1981. I find that children and pretty sophisticated and appreciate authenticity. However, I would speak to a group of kindergartners much different that middle-schoolers. They are at different parts of the story.
**_Remember_ is one of your early poems. How has it been watching _Remember_ grow a life of its own?**
I would never have guessed that Remember would have such legs, such wings. To me, it was a humble poem, by a young Native poet trying to understand and work with this discipline, this art called “poetry.” I never planned to be a poet. And I had to find my own way. That’s the path of an artist.
**Are there any other poems of yours you would like to see in picture book format?**

I have several ideas for children’s books, and have a couple of ideas for a children’s book series. “Perhaps the World Ends Here” might make a good children’s book, though I’d have to revise a couple of lines.
**Tell me about the collaboration process with Michaela Goade. How did you align your vision of the poem with her vision for the visual spirit of the work?**
Michael Goade was my first choice as an artist. During our discussion about the art she said she could research my Mvskoke people’s culture, then she asked about the possibility of exploring the poem through her own Tlingit culture. I told her to go with what inspires her. And she did!
I had a wonderful mentor and friend from her culture, the poet and culture bearer Nora Dauenhauer. I like to think of this collaboration as an acknowledgement of our connection. The book is a bridge between families, and as the message of the poem reveals, ultimately we are all related.
SXSW-EDU with Michaela Goade and Mandy Smoker.
_Cynsational Notes:_
Joy Har­jo, the 23 rd Poet Lau­re­ate of the Unit­ed States, is a mem­ber of the Mvskoke Nation. She is only the sec­ond poet to be appoint­ed a third term as U.S. Poet Laureate. Born in Tul­sa, Okla­homa, she left home to attend high school at the inno­v­a­tive Insti­tute of Amer­i­can Indi­an Arts, which was then a Bureau of Indi­an Affairs school.

Har­jo is the author of ten books of poet­ry, includ­ing her most recent,Weav­ing Sun­down in a Scar­let Light: Fifty Poems for Fifty Years(W. W. Norton & Company 2022), the high­ly acclaimedAn Amer­i­can Sun­rise(W. W. Norton & Company, 2019), which was a 2020 Okla­homa Book Award Win­ner,Con­flict Res­o­lu­tion for Holy Beings(W. W. Norton & Company, 2015), which was short­list­ed for the Grif­fin Prize and named a Notable Book of the Year by the Amer­i­can Library Asso­ci­a­tion, andIn Mad Love and War(Wesleyan University Press, 1990), which received an Amer­i­can Book Award and the Del­more Schwartz Memo­r­i­al Award.
Her first mem­oir,Crazy Brave (W. W. Norton & Company, 2013), was award­ed the PEN USA Lit­er­ary Award in Cre­ative Non Fic­tion and the Amer­i­can Book Award, and her sec­ond,Poet War­rior: A Mem­oir (W. W. Norton & Company, 2021). She has pub­lished three award-win­n­ing children’s books, Remem­ber(Random House, 2023) The Good Luck Cat(Houghton Mifflin, 2000) and For a Girl Becom­ing (University of Arizona Press, 2009)
In addi­tion to serv­ing as a three-term U.S. Poet Lau­re­ate, Har­jo is a chan­cel­lor of the Acad­e­my of Amer­i­can Poets and is a found­ing board mem­ber and Chair of the Native Arts and Cul­tures Foun­da­tion. She has recent­ly been induct­ed into the Amer­i­can Acad­e­my of Arts and Let­ters, the Amer­i­can Philo­soph­i­cal Soci­ety, the Nation­al Native Amer­i­can Hall of Fame, and the Nation­al Woman’s Hall of Fame.

She lives in Tul­sa, Okla­homa where she is the inau­gur­al Artist-in-Res­i­dence of the Bob Dylan Center.
AJ Eversole grew up in rural Oklahoma, a place removed from city life and full of opportunities to grow the imagination, which she did through intense games of make believe. She graduated from Oklahoma State University. She is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma and hopes to be traditionally published in the near future. She currently resides in Fort Worth, Texas with her husband and son. Visit her on Twitter: @amjoyeversole and Instagram: @ajeversole

**Mary Jane Oliver** (September 10, 1935 – January 17, 2019) was an American poet who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984 and the National Book Award in 1992. She found inspiration for her work in nature and had a lifelong habit of solitary walks in the wild. Her poetry is characterized by wonderment at the natural environment, vivid imagery, spirituality, and unadorned language. Oliver is one of the best-selling poets in American history.
Mary Oliver was born to Edward William and Helen M. Oliver on September 10, 1935, in Maple Heights, Ohio, a semi-rural suburb of Cleveland.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1) Her father was a social studies teacher and athletics coach in the Cleveland public schools. As a child, she spent a great deal of time outside, going on walks or reading. In an interview with _The Christian Science Monitor_ in 1992, Oliver said of growing up in Ohio:
> It was pastoral, it was nice, it was an extended family. I don't know why I felt such an affinity with the natural world except that it was available to me. That's the first thing. It was right there. And for whatever reasons, I felt those first important connections, those first experiences being made with the natural world rather than with the social world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-:1-2)

In a 2011 interview with Maria Shriver, Oliver said she had been sexually abused as a child and had experienced recurring nightmares.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-3) Oliver called her family dysfunctional, adding that though her childhood was very hard, writing helped her create her own world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-4)
Oliver began writing poetry at the age of 14. She graduated from the local high school in Maple Heights. In the summer of 1951, at age 15, she attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen, Michigan, now known as Interlochen Arts Camp, where she was in the percussion section of the National High School Orchestra. At 17, she visited the home of the Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, in Austerlitz, New York,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) where she formed a friendship with the late poet's sister Norma. Oliver spent the next six to seven years at the estate helping Norma organize Edna St. Vincent Millay's papers.
Oliver studied at Ohio State University and Vassar College in the mid-1950s but did not receive a degree at either college.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)

Oliver worked at ''Steepletop'', Edna St. Vincent Millay's estate, as secretary to the poet's sister.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-6) Her first collection of poems, _No Voyage, and Other Poems_, was published in 1963, when she was 28.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) During the early 1980s, Oliver taught at Case Western Reserve University. Her fifth collection of poetry, _American Primitive_, won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1984.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-8)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-pulitzer-9) She was Poet In Residence at Bucknell University (1986) and Margaret Banister Writer in Residence at Sweet Briar College (1991), then moved to Bennington, Vermont, where she held the Catharine Osgood Foster Chair for Distinguished Teaching at Bennington College until 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7)

She won the Christopher Award and the L. L. Winship/PEN New England Award for _House of Light_ (1990), and _New and Selected Poems_ (1992) won the National Book Award.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-nba1992-10) Oliver's work turns to nature for inspiration and describes the sense of wonder it instilled in her. "When it's over" she wrote, "I want to say: all my life / I was a bride married to amazement. I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms" ("When Death Comes" from _New and Selected Poems_). Her collections _Winter Hours: Prose, Prose Poems, and Poems_ (1999), _Why I Wake Early_ (2004), and _New and Selected Poems, Volume 2_ (2004) build the themes. The first and second parts of _Leaf and the Cloud_ are featured in _The Best American Poetry_1999 and 2000,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-AAP-11) and her essays appear in _Best American Essays_ 1996, 1998, and 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) Oliver was the editor of the 2009 edition of _Best American Essays._
Other awards she received include the Lannan Literary Award and the Pioneer Award from the Santa Monica Public Library Green Prize for Sustainable Literature. She was awarded honorary doctorates from Marquette University (2012), Tufts University (2008), Dartmouth College (2007), and The Art Institute of Boston (1998).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-12)

In 2007, _The New York Times_ called Oliver "far and away, this country's best-selling poet."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Gardner2007-13)
Oliver's poetry is grounded in memories of Ohio and her adopted home of New England. Provincetown is the principal setting for her work after she moved there in the 1960s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) Influenced by both Whitman and Thoreau, she is known for her clear and poignant observations of the natural world. According to the 1983 Chronology of American Literature, her collection _American Primitive_ "presents a new kind of Romanticism that refuses to acknowledge boundaries between nature and the observing self."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-14) Nature stirred her creativity, and Oliver, an avid walker, often pursued inspiration on foot. Her poems are filled with imagery from her daily walks near her home:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) shore birds, water snakes, the phases of the moon, and humpback whales. In _Long Life_, she writes, "[I] go off to my woods, my ponds, my sun-filled harbor, no more than a blue comma on the map of the world but, to me, the emblem of everything."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) She once said: "When things are going well, you know, the walk does not get rapid or get anywhere: I finally just stop and write.

**Mary Jane Oliver** (September 10, 1935 – January 17, 2019) was an American poet who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984 and the National Book Award in 1992. She found inspiration for her work in nature and had a lifelong habit of solitary walks in the wild. Her poetry is characterized by wonderment at the natural environment, vivid imagery, spirituality, and unadorned language. Oliver is one of the best-selling poets in American history.
Mary Oliver was born to Edward William and Helen M. Oliver on September 10, 1935, in Maple Heights, Ohio, a semi-rural suburb of Cleveland.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1) Her father was a social studies teacher and athletics coach in the Cleveland public schools. As a child, she spent a great deal of time outside, going on walks or reading. In an interview with _The Christian Science Monitor_ in 1992, Oliver said of growing up in Ohio:
> It was pastoral, it was nice, it was an extended family. I don't know why I felt such an affinity with the natural world except that it was available to me. That's the first thing. It was right there. And for whatever reasons, I felt those first important connections, those first experiences being made with the natural world rather than with the social world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-:1-2)
texts.1:
In a 2011 interview with Maria Shriver, Oliver said she had been sexually abused as a child and had experienced recurring nightmares.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-3) Oliver called her family dysfunctional, adding that though her childhood was very hard, writing helped her create her own world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-4)
Oliver began writing poetry at the age of 14. She graduated from the local high school in Maple Heights. In the summer of 1951, at age 15, she attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen, Michigan, now known as Interlochen Arts Camp, where she was in the percussion section of the National High School Orchestra. At 17, she visited the home of the Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, in Austerlitz, New York,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) where she formed a friendship with the late poet's sister Norma. Oliver spent the next six to seven years at the estate helping Norma organize Edna St. Vincent Millay's papers.
Oliver studied at Ohio State University and Vassar College in the mid-1950s but did not receive a degree at either college.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)
texts.2: Oliver worked at ''Steepletop'', Edna St. Vincent Millay's estate, as secretary to the poet's sister.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-6) Her first collection of poems, _No Voyage, and Other Poems_, was published in 1963, when she was 28.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) During the early 1980s, Oliver taught at Case Western Reserve University. Her fifth collection of poetry, _American Primitive_, won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1984.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-8)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-pulitzer-9) She was Poet In Residence at Bucknell University (1986) and Margaret Banister Writer in Residence at Sweet Briar College (1991), then moved to Bennington, Vermont, where she held the Catharine Osgood Foster Chair for Distinguished Teaching at Bennington College until 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7)
texts.3:
She won the Christopher Award and the L. L. Winship/PEN New England Award for _House of Light_ (1990), and _New and Selected Poems_ (1992) won the National Book Award.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-nba1992-10) Oliver's work turns to nature for inspiration and describes the sense of wonder it instilled in her. "When it's over" she wrote, "I want to say: all my life / I was a bride married to amazement. I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms" ("When Death Comes" from _New and Selected Poems_). Her collections _Winter Hours: Prose, Prose Poems, and Poems_ (1999), _Why I Wake Early_ (2004), and _New and Selected Poems, Volume 2_ (2004) build the themes. The first and second parts of _Leaf and the Cloud_ are featured in _The Best American Poetry_1999 and 2000,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-AAP-11) and her essays appear in _Best American Essays_ 1996, 1998, and 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) Oliver was the editor of the 2009 edition of _Best American Essays._
Other awards she received include the Lannan Literary Award and the Pioneer Award from the Santa Monica Public Library Green Prize for Sustainable Literature. She was awarded honorary doctorates from Marquette University (2012), Tufts University (2008), Dartmouth College (2007), and The Art Institute of Boston (1998).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-12)
texts.4:
In 2007, _The New York Times_ called Oliver "far and away, this country's best-selling poet."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Gardner2007-13)
Oliver's poetry is grounded in memories of Ohio and her adopted home of New England. Provincetown is the principal setting for her work after she moved there in the 1960s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) Influenced by both Whitman and Thoreau, she is known for her clear and poignant observations of the natural world. According to the 1983 Chronology of American Literature, her collection _American Primitive_ "presents a new kind of Romanticism that refuses to acknowledge boundaries between nature and the observing self."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-14) Nature stirred her creativity, and Oliver, an avid walker, often pursued inspiration on foot. Her poems are filled with imagery from her daily walks near her home:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) shore birds, water snakes, the phases of the moon, and humpback whales. In _Long Life_, she writes, "[I] go off to my woods, my ponds, my sun-filled harbor, no more than a blue comma on the map of the world but, to me, the emblem of everything."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) She once said: "When things are going well, you know, the walk does not get rapid or get anywhere: I finally just stop and write.

By AJ Eversole
Today on Cynsations I am thrilled to present an interview with former, U.S. Poet Laureate, Joy Harjo. Her latest picture book, _Remember_ (Random House Studio, 2023) released last week. Illustrated by Caldecott Medalist Michaela Goade,_Remember_, is a poem in picture book form.
**What is the heart of _Remember_?**
I used to ask this of my creative writing students when I taught. The heart of this poem can be found by the rhythm, the beat that runs through and is repeated in the word “Remember.” It pumps life in the poem. The driving force reminds us that are all connected and ultimately we are earth or Ekvnvcvke.
**What do you think of children as an audience for poetry?**
Children can be natural poets in that they naturally play with whatever materials are at hand. Word play is a given. They like ear surprises, respond to rhythm and music. They love poetry and when given a change to make their own poems are usually eager to participate.
**Do children as an audience change the way you package or present a poem?**
I think this depends on the age and the poem. I did not write the poem “Remember” specifically for children. The poem was in response to a request to write a poem to advise younger up-and-coming poets, when I was but a younger and up-and-coming poet myself. I wrote the poem in the seventies. It was published in my first book She Had Some Horses (W. W. Norton) which was published in 1981. I find that children and pretty sophisticated and appreciate authenticity. However, I would speak to a group of kindergartners much different that middle-schoolers. They are at different parts of the story.
**_Remember_ is one of your early poems. How has it been watching _Remember_ grow a life of its own?**
I would never have guessed that Remember would have such legs, such wings. To me, it was a humble poem, by a young Native poet trying to understand and work with this discipline, this art called “poetry.” I never planned to be a poet. And I had to find my own way. That’s the path of an artist.
**Are there any other poems of yours you would like to see in picture book format?**
texts.1:
I have several ideas for children’s books, and have a couple of ideas for a children’s book series. “Perhaps the World Ends Here” might make a good children’s book, though I’d have to revise a couple of lines.
**Tell me about the collaboration process with Michaela Goade. How did you align your vision of the poem with her vision for the visual spirit of the work?**
Michael Goade was my first choice as an artist. During our discussion about the art she said she could research my Mvskoke people’s culture, then she asked about the possibility of exploring the poem through her own Tlingit culture. I told her to go with what inspires her. And she did!
I had a wonderful mentor and friend from her culture, the poet and culture bearer Nora Dauenhauer. I like to think of this collaboration as an acknowledgement of our connection. The book is a bridge between families, and as the message of the poem reveals, ultimately we are all related.
SXSW-EDU with Michaela Goade and Mandy Smoker.
_Cynsational Notes:_
Joy Har­jo, the 23 rd Poet Lau­re­ate of the Unit­ed States, is a mem­ber of the Mvskoke Nation. She is only the sec­ond poet to be appoint­ed a third term as U.S. Poet Laureate. Born in Tul­sa, Okla­homa, she left home to attend high school at the inno­v­a­tive Insti­tute of Amer­i­can Indi­an Arts, which was then a Bureau of Indi­an Affairs school.
texts.2:
Har­jo is the author of ten books of poet­ry, includ­ing her most recent,Weav­ing Sun­down in a Scar­let Light: Fifty Poems for Fifty Years(W. W. Norton & Company 2022), the high­ly acclaimedAn Amer­i­can Sun­rise(W. W. Norton & Company, 2019), which was a 2020 Okla­homa Book Award Win­ner,Con­flict Res­o­lu­tion for Holy Beings(W. W. Norton & Company, 2015), which was short­list­ed for the Grif­fin Prize and named a Notable Book of the Year by the Amer­i­can Library Asso­ci­a­tion, andIn Mad Love and War(Wesleyan University Press, 1990), which received an Amer­i­can Book Award and the Del­more Schwartz Memo­r­i­al Award.
Her first mem­oir,Crazy Brave (W. W. Norton & Company, 2013), was award­ed the PEN USA Lit­er­ary Award in Cre­ative Non Fic­tion and the Amer­i­can Book Award, and her sec­ond,Poet War­rior: A Mem­oir (W. W. Norton & Company, 2021). She has pub­lished three award-win­n­ing children’s books, Remem­ber(Random House, 2023) The Good Luck Cat(Houghton Mifflin, 2000) and For a Girl Becom­ing (University of Arizona Press, 2009)
In addi­tion to serv­ing as a three-term U.S. Poet Lau­re­ate, Har­jo is a chan­cel­lor of the Acad­e­my of Amer­i­can Poets and is a found­ing board mem­ber and Chair of the Native Arts and Cul­tures Foun­da­tion. She has recent­ly been induct­ed into the Amer­i­can Acad­e­my of Arts and Let­ters, the Amer­i­can Philo­soph­i­cal Soci­ety, the Nation­al Native Amer­i­can Hall of Fame, and the Nation­al Woman’s Hall of Fame.
texts.3:
She lives in Tul­sa, Okla­homa where she is the inau­gur­al Artist-in-Res­i­dence of the Bob Dylan Center.
AJ Eversole grew up in rural Oklahoma, a place removed from city life and full of opportunities to grow the imagination, which she did through intense games of make believe. She graduated from Oklahoma State University. She is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma and hopes to be traditionally published in the near future. She currently resides in Fort Worth, Texas with her husband and son. Visit her on Twitter: @amjoyeversole and Instagram: @ajeversole

**Mary Jane Oliver** (September 10, 1935 – January 17, 2019) was an American poet who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984 and the National Book Award in 1992. She found inspiration for her work in nature and had a lifelong habit of solitary walks in the wild. Her poetry is characterized by wonderment at the natural environment, vivid imagery, spirituality, and unadorned language. Oliver is one of the best-selling poets in American history.
Mary Oliver was born to Edward William and Helen M. Oliver on September 10, 1935, in Maple Heights, Ohio, a semi-rural suburb of Cleveland.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1) Her father was a social studies teacher and athletics coach in the Cleveland public schools. As a child, she spent a great deal of time outside, going on walks or reading. In an interview with _The Christian Science Monitor_ in 1992, Oliver said of growing up in Ohio:
> It was pastoral, it was nice, it was an extended family. I don't know why I felt such an affinity with the natural world except that it was available to me. That's the first thing. It was right there. And for whatever reasons, I felt those first important connections, those first experiences being made with the natural world rather than with the social world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-:1-2)

In a 2011 interview with Maria Shriver, Oliver said she had been sexually abused as a child and had experienced recurring nightmares.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-3) Oliver called her family dysfunctional, adding that though her childhood was very hard, writing helped her create her own world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-4)
Oliver began writing poetry at the age of 14. She graduated from the local high school in Maple Heights. In the summer of 1951, at age 15, she attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen, Michigan, now known as Interlochen Arts Camp, where she was in the percussion section of the National High School Orchestra. At 17, she visited the home of the Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, in Austerlitz, New York,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) where she formed a friendship with the late poet's sister Norma. Oliver spent the next six to seven years at the estate helping Norma organize Edna St. Vincent Millay's papers.
Oliver studied at Ohio State University and Vassar College in the mid-1950s but did not receive a degree at either college.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)

Oliver worked at ''Steepletop'', Edna St. Vincent Millay's estate, as secretary to the poet's sister.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-6) Her first collection of poems, _No Voyage, and Other Poems_, was published in 1963, when she was 28.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) During the early 1980s, Oliver taught at Case Western Reserve University. Her fifth collection of poetry, _American Primitive_, won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1984.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-8)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-pulitzer-9) She was Poet In Residence at Bucknell University (1986) and Margaret Banister Writer in Residence at Sweet Briar College (1991), then moved to Bennington, Vermont, where she held the Catharine Osgood Foster Chair for Distinguished Teaching at Bennington College until 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7)

She won the Christopher Award and the L. L. Winship/PEN New England Award for _House of Light_ (1990), and _New and Selected Poems_ (1992) won the National Book Award.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-PoetryFound-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-nba1992-10) Oliver's work turns to nature for inspiration and describes the sense of wonder it instilled in her. "When it's over" she wrote, "I want to say: all my life / I was a bride married to amazement. I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms" ("When Death Comes" from _New and Selected Poems_). Her collections _Winter Hours: Prose, Prose Poems, and Poems_ (1999), _Why I Wake Early_ (2004), and _New and Selected Poems, Volume 2_ (2004) build the themes. The first and second parts of _Leaf and the Cloud_ are featured in _The Best American Poetry_1999 and 2000,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-AAP-11) and her essays appear in _Best American Essays_ 1996, 1998, and 2001.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) Oliver was the editor of the 2009 edition of _Best American Essays._
Other awards she received include the Lannan Literary Award and the Pioneer Award from the Santa Monica Public Library Green Prize for Sustainable Literature. She was awarded honorary doctorates from Marquette University (2012), Tufts University (2008), Dartmouth College (2007), and The Art Institute of Boston (1998).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-12)

In 2007, _The New York Times_ called Oliver "far and away, this country's best-selling poet."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Gardner2007-13)
Oliver's poetry is grounded in memories of Ohio and her adopted home of New England. Provincetown is the principal setting for her work after she moved there in the 1960s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) Influenced by both Whitman and Thoreau, she is known for her clear and poignant observations of the natural world. According to the 1983 Chronology of American Literature, her collection _American Primitive_ "presents a new kind of Romanticism that refuses to acknowledge boundaries between nature and the observing self."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-14) Nature stirred her creativity, and Oliver, an avid walker, often pursued inspiration on foot. Her poems are filled with imagery from her daily walks near her home:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Beaconpress-7) shore birds, water snakes, the phases of the moon, and humpback whales. In _Long Life_, she writes, "[I] go off to my woods, my ponds, my sun-filled harbor, no more than a blue comma on the map of the world but, to me, the emblem of everything."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Oliver#cite_note-Land-5) She once said: "When things are going well, you know, the walk does not get rapid or get anywhere: I finally just stop and write.

Title: Author Interview: Joy Harjo on Poetry & Picture Books

By AJ Eversole
Today on Cynsations I am thrilled to present an interview with former, U.S. Poet Laureate, Joy Harjo. Her latest picture book, _Remember_ (Random House Studio, 2023) released last week. Illustrated by Caldecott Medalist Michaela Goade,_Remember_, is a poem in picture book form.
**What is the heart of _Remember_?**
I used to ask this of my creative writing students when I taught. The heart of this poem can be found by the rhythm, the beat that runs through and is repeated in the word “Remember.” It pumps life in the poem. The driving force reminds us that are all connected and ultimately we are earth or Ekvnvcvke.
**What do you think of children as an audience for poetry?**
Children can be natural poets in that they naturally play with whatever materials are at hand. Word play is a given. They like ear surprises, respond to rhythm and music. They love poetry and when given a change to make their own poems are usually eager to participate.
**Do children as an audience change the way you package or present a poem?**
I think this depends on the age and the poem. I did not write the poem “Remember” specifically for children. The poem was in response to a request to write a poem to advise younger up-and-coming poets, when I was but a younger and up-and-coming poet myself. I wrote the poem in the seventies. It was published in my first book She Had Some Horses (W. W. Norton) which was published in 1981. I find that children and pretty sophisticated and appreciate authenticity. However, I would speak to a group of kindergartners much different that middle-schoolers. They are at different parts of the story.
**_Remember_ is one of your early poems. How has it been watching _Remember_ grow a life of its own?**
I would never have guessed that Remember would have such legs, such wings. To me, it was a humble poem, by a young Native poet trying to understand and work with this discipline, this art called “poetry.” I never planned to be a poet. And I had to find my own way. That’s the path of an artist.
**Are there any other poems of yours you would like to see in picture book format?**

I have several ideas for children’s books, and have a couple of ideas for a children’s book series. “Perhaps the World Ends Here” might make a good children’s book, though I’d have to revise a couple of lines.
**Tell me about the collaboration process with Michaela Goade. How did you align your vision of the poem with her vision for the visual spirit of the work?**
Michael Goade was my first choice as an artist. During our discussion about the art she said she could research my Mvskoke people’s culture, then she asked about the possibility of exploring the poem through her own Tlingit culture. I told her to go with what inspires her. And she did!
I had a wonderful mentor and friend from her culture, the poet and culture bearer Nora Dauenhauer. I like to think of this collaboration as an acknowledgement of our connection. The book is a bridge between families, and as the message of the poem reveals, ultimately we are all related.
SXSW-EDU with Michaela Goade and Mandy Smoker.
_Cynsational Notes:_
Joy Har­jo, the 23 rd Poet Lau­re­ate of the Unit­ed States, is a mem­ber of the Mvskoke Nation. She is only the sec­ond poet to be appoint­ed a third term as U.S. Poet Laureate. Born in Tul­sa, Okla­homa, she left home to attend high school at the inno­v­a­tive Insti­tute of Amer­i­can Indi­an Arts, which was then a Bureau of Indi­an Affairs school.

Har­jo is the author of ten books of poet­ry, includ­ing her most recent,Weav­ing Sun­down in a Scar­let Light: Fifty Poems for Fifty Years(W. W. Norton & Company 2022), the high­ly acclaimedAn Amer­i­can Sun­rise(W. W. Norton & Company, 2019), which was a 2020 Okla­homa Book Award Win­ner,Con­flict Res­o­lu­tion for Holy Beings(W. W. Norton & Company, 2015), which was short­list­ed for the Grif­fin Prize and named a Notable Book of the Year by the Amer­i­can Library Asso­ci­a­tion, andIn Mad Love and War(Wesleyan University Press, 1990), which received an Amer­i­can Book Award and the Del­more Schwartz Memo­r­i­al Award.
Her first mem­oir,Crazy Brave (W. W. Norton & Company, 2013), was award­ed the PEN USA Lit­er­ary Award in Cre­ative Non Fic­tion and the Amer­i­can Book Award, and her sec­ond,Poet War­rior: A Mem­oir (W. W. Norton & Company, 2021). She has pub­lished three award-win­n­ing children’s books, Remem­ber(Random House, 2023) The Good Luck Cat(Houghton Mifflin, 2000) and For a Girl Becom­ing (University of Arizona Press, 2009)
In addi­tion to serv­ing as a three-term U.S. Poet Lau­re­ate, Har­jo is a chan­cel­lor of the Acad­e­my of Amer­i­can Poets and is a found­ing board mem­ber and Chair of the Native Arts and Cul­tures Foun­da­tion. She has recent­ly been induct­ed into the Amer­i­can Acad­e­my of Arts and Let­ters, the Amer­i­can Philo­soph­i­cal Soci­ety, the Nation­al Native Amer­i­can Hall of Fame, and the Nation­al Woman’s Hall of Fame.

She lives in Tul­sa, Okla­homa where she is the inau­gur­al Artist-in-Res­i­dence of the Bob Dylan Center.
AJ Eversole grew up in rural Oklahoma, a place removed from city life and full of opportunities to grow the imagination, which she did through intense games of make believe. She graduated from Oklahoma State University. She is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma and hopes to be traditionally published in the near future. She currently resides in Fort Worth, Texas with her husband and son. Visit her on Twitter: @amjoyeversole and Instagram: @ajeversole

Source: https://robertcharboneau.substack.com/p/maya-popa-is-a-hopeless-romantic
Title: Maya Popa is a Hopeless Romantic
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,14,15,16,17,18
What is the major voice in American poetry today? What is the popular style? What is that generic contemporary idiom such that, if one would hear with the ears closed, picturing with the aural imagination, they would hear its tone of voice? What would such a voice sound like, and what would it suggest? What would we hear in its pitch and stress, in its timbre, in the manner of its cadences and in the arguments of its melodies?
Robert Frost called such hearing the sound of sense. “The abstract vitality of our speech.” It’s what we can intuit from conversations overheard from behind a wall or across a café. The tunes one remembers without remembering all the words.
If you squinted at contemporary poetry with your ears, you might at first audially imagine many different styles. The softspokenness of an academic, the rhythm of a spoken word poet at an open mic, the earnestness of a teenager in front of a phone screen. Whatever you imagined, the generic voice would probably sound a bit like all of these. It would sound, as with all poetry, elevated in manner from regular speech. Its language would be ostentatious, suggesting more than in prose. Conversational, plainspoken, yet lyrical. It would speak with candor about the personal, yet it would be highly impressionistic and self-conscious. It would be written in free verse, and it would not rhyme, but it would be ‘sonic.’ It would aim at self-expression and powerful feeling above all else. Its character would be essentially romantic, as the major American mode has always been.
I imagine, above all, someone like Mary Oliver. Popular since the 80s, she remains beloved and imitated. Her influence can be felt from academia to Instagram. Her expressions permeate the popular culture. A new documentary out this year about her life, _Saved by the Beauty of the World,_ positions Oliver as the poet who’s read by people who don’t like poetry. It features celebrity champions of poetry like Helena Bonham Carter, Stephen Colbert, and Oprah Winfrey. Oliver is undoubtedly a conduit of the tradition. Her style draws from many strands, making something homogeneous and mainstream. Her writing is accessible and her sentiments about nature and beauty seem quintessential to poetry. Generically beautiful, intimate, poignant, feminine, romantic.

If I had to picture which voice most closely resembles that style today, I would picture Maya Popa. I would hear in my mind’s ear Maya Popa’s voice. She is, I think, an heir to Mary Oliver, perhaps _the_ heir, and her newest collection, _If You Love That Lady_ (Norton), sounds like the major American idiom of the last few decades.
Though she does not have the popularity of Kaur or Gorman or Vuong, Popa has nevertheless achieved success in the poetry world. She is published by Norton, and regularly appears in major trad magazines like _The New Yorker_, _The Atlantic_, and _The Guardian_. She’s an editor for _Publisher’s Weekly_. She’s escaped the confines of academia and MFA programs (though she is the product of an MFA from NYU) and found mainstream success through Substack (22,000+ subscribers) and the Conscious Writers Collective. Her website says she’s been commissioned by major institutions including the United Nations, the Grotte de Lazaret, and Van Cleef & Arpels. She has a broad reading audience beyond poets themselves, and is popular for the same reasons as Oliver: her style is accessible, and her message, whether of enchantment, desire, or mortality, is a simple and perennial one.
Maya Popa is part of the American romantic tradition that has been the dominant poetic voice in the country since its founding. Indeed, American poetry has always been the child of the English Romantics. We had our Augustan imitators, poets of the Revolution like Freneau and the Connecticut Wits, but in the first decades after independence, when America was still in its infancy, still forming its identity, English Romanticism was ascendant. American poets adopted the style because it was fashionable, but also because its spirit was really our spirit. Born of radical Enlightenment principles, but democratic and less sophisticated than our European counterparts, we naturally preferred self-reliance and instinct over reason. Protestantism taught us to listen to our hearts and trust our intuitions, and the natural world, the Frontier, was an ever-present part of the American condition. This was the place for the Romanticism, and so the style of Pope naturally gave way to the style of Wordsworth. We traded neoclassicism for naturalism, and heroic couplets for blank verse.

Our first popular poet, William Cullen Bryant was a self-acknowledged student of Wordsworth. Now mostly forgotten, he was in his time a sensation, as renowned as Charles Dickens, who he entertained on a visit to New York in 1842. Dickens’ first question upon arriving in America was “Where is Bryant?” Edgar Allen Poe, too, wrote of Bryant with reverence. “In character no man stands more loftily… The peculiarly melancholy expression of his countenance has caused him to be accused of harshness, or coldness of heart. Never was there a greater mistake. His soul is charity itself, in all respects generous and noble.” Bryant went on walking tours abroad with Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Walter Savage Landor, and Robert and Elizabeth Browning. He knew James Fenimore Cooper, Fitz-Greene Halleck, and Thomas Cole. He was editor of the _New York Review_ and the _New York_ _Evening Post_. He edited the _Library of Poetry and Song_, a massive anthology of English and American verse. He was the first American to translate Homer. He advocated for international copyright protection. He even met with Andrew Jackson and advised Lincoln on cabinet appointments in 1861. He was, in short, an integral part of the culture. Above all, Bryant embodied the American man of letters and helped forge the American literary character. And it was to be a thoroughly romantic one.
His greatest poem, “Thanatopsis,” written when he was only 18, begins by introducing the essential Wordsworthian man
> To him who in the love of nature holds  
>   
> Communion with her visible forms, she speaks  
>   
> A various language

A meditation on death, Bryant urges us, when “thoughts of the last bitter hour come like a blight” on our spirits, to go into the woods and “list to Nature’s teachings.” Bryant’s narrators frequently implore us to escape into nature, or are escaping themselves. His subjects are the fairy music of green rivers, the solitude and splendor of winter woods, the summer wind, spring fountains, the heart-swelling vistas of prairies. His best poems are all variations on the theme of Nature’s restorative and instructive powers. He was hardly original in this, and the vividness of his descriptions are never as striking, nor his insights as deep or nuanced, as those of Wordsworth’s. But his career and work established in American poetry a voice that would carry through the transcendentalists down to Mary Oliver.
> My heart is awed within me, when I think  
>   
> Of the great miracle that still goes on,  
>   
> In silence, round me—the perpetual work  
>   
> Of thy creation, finished, yet renewed  
>   
> Forever. Written on thy works I read  
>   
> The lesson of thy own eternity.  
>   
> Lo! all grow old and die—but see, again,  
>   
> How on the faltering footsteps of decay  
>   
> Youth presses—ever gay and beautiful youth  
>   
> In all its beautiful forms. These lofty trees  
>   
> Wave not less proudly that their ancestors  
>   
> Moulder beneath them.  
>   
>   
> —from “Forest Hymn”
Oliver is as unoriginal as Bryant in this sense. Both preoccupied with nature and mortality and the relationship between them, both immensely popular because of their plain style and the simplicity of their ideas. Popa exists firmly within this tradition, and has since her previous book, _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ (Norton, 2022).

> The trees were on the verge of rebirth so sudden  
>   
> you’d miss it from one day to the next,  
>   
>   
> would be suddenly alive in it, the pale green bending open  
>   
> to reveal what we’d always suspected was the case:  
>   
>   
> that every bright thing has at its heart a hiddenness  
>   
> it offers when you’ve just about stopped looking.  
>   
>   
> from “All That Is Made”
Popa’s interest in the natural world is reparative, like Bryant’s. _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is about healing, whether from illness, the pandemic, death, loss. It’s about the ways in which suffering can open one up to feelings of awe. She tells us in “All Inner Life Runs At Some Delay” that “_Wound is where the light enters_,” a phrase she attributes to Rumi. Her new book, _If You Love That Lady_, is also about loss, the breaking off of a marriage that leaves the poet wandering in “the remainder of a life that love had made.”
The book’s title comes from a quote from Robert Graves’ advice to Siegfried Sassoon: “If you love that lady, don’t marry her.” It’s also the title of a collection of courtship letters between Sally McDowell and John Miller, which Popa tells us several of the poems were drawn from. McDowell was a 19th century Maryland socialite, the wife of the governor, who was accused by her jealous husband (who was 20 years her senior) of infidelity, and whose reputation was ruined by the accusations which the husband made public in a 52-page pamphlet which he distributed, incredibly, to all of Congress. McDowell was humiliated and ostracized. Afterwards she developed a relationship with John Miller, a Presbyterian minister, through a series of letters, and eventually the two married.

The letters show a woman struggling after public humiliation to let herself be loved again. The speaker in Popa’s collection, too, struggles to pick up the pieces of herself. She wanders through various cities and fragments of memories, with more ennui and with less focus than Popa’s previous effort, although with a familiar wound. The grief in _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is not unlike the heartbreak in _If You Love That Lady_. The basic presentation of suffering remains the same. It is elusive, elliptical, abstract. Always the hum of thoughts evaded by the mind. Familiar in the way it uses apostrophes addressed to “you,” in the way the unidentified pronouns fill the poems with a sense of intimacy. And although the presence of the natural world is somewhat diminished compared to _Wound_ (the style of _If You Love That Lady_ overall feels ‘diminished’) Popa continues to express a sensibility which is the inheritance of her romantic forbears. She embodies the American romantic in subject, sensibility, and in those theories that undergird romantic poetry.
The romantic theory prevalent in poetry operates under that assumption that literature is mainly or even purely an emotional experience. It often opposes the emotional to the rational, the emotional being ultimately good and desirable, while the rational is something to be looked on with suspicion. So in “The Conjunction of Jupiter and Venus,” William Cullen Bryant sets emotion and reason on the scale and weighs them against one another.
> I would not always reason. The straight path  
>   
> Wearies us with its never-varying lines,  
>   
> And we grow melancholy. I would make  
>   
> Reason my guide, but she should sometimes sit  
>   
> Patiently by the way-side, while I traced  
>   
> The mazes of the pleasant wilderness  
>   
> Around me. She should be my counsellor,  
>   
> But not my tyrant. For the spirit needs  
>   
> Impulses from a deeper source than hers,  
>   
> And there are motions, in the mind of man,  
>   
> That she must look upon with awe. I bow  
>   
> Reverently to her dictates, but not less  
>   
> Hold to the fair illusions of old time—  
>   
> Illusions that shed brightness over life,  
>   
> And glory over nature.

Bryant would make reason his guide, but he would not always follow its straight path, for there is something outside reason, beyond it. “Impulses from a deeper source than hers.” He calls them “Illusions that shed brightness over life, And glory over nature.” They are the source of life itself, invigorating and inspiring us. We experience them in moments of intense emotion. They are intuitive and irrational. One often encounters them in nature.
Mary Oliver describes something similar in “The Black Snake.” Upon finding a snake dead on the side of the road, struck by a driver, she pulls over to move its “looped and useless” body out of the way, and in the moment contemplates death
> its suddenness,  
>   
> its terrible weight,  
>   
> its certain coming. Yet under  
>   
>   
> reason burns a brighter fire, which the bones  
>   
> have always preferred.  
>   
> It is the story of endless good fortune.  
>   
> It says to oblivion: not me!  
>   
>   
> It is the light at the center of every cell.  
>   
> It is what sent the snake coiling and flowing forward  
>   
> happily all spring through the green leaves before  
>   
> he came to the road.
Oliver, like Bryant, opposes this animating force to reason. It is underneath reason and “burns a brighter fire, which the bones have always preferred.” She encounters it, like Bryant, in nature. The road, meanwhile, which is manmade, is unnatural. It is part of the ordered world of civilization. It is what killed the snake who, before it slithered out onto it, was “coiling and flowing forward happily all spring.” It is the same straight path of reason which Bryant, in his poem, would not always follow. So both poets maintain an essentially romantic outlook which identifies the good with feeling and nature, the bad with reason and civilization.
Whereas Bryant is skeptical of reason, recognizing its limitations, yet practical in his desire to join it with feeling, Oliver is more dismissive of reason. She has no use for it. In “What is There Beyond Knowing” she tells us

It is an understanding which does not seek to understand, but to simply be, to exist, without thinking. It is a call to slow down and breathe. Simple and plain. As the poem which begins the third and final section, “The World” marks a transition in the narrative arc of _If You Love That Lady_ that will conclude with the final lines of “It All Comes Back To Me Now,” lines that lift and make light of that weight of grief the poet has been carrying throughout:
> Here I am, filled out by happiness  
>   
> I could not otherwise have earned.  
>   
>   
> God forbid I hadn’t taken every last wrong turn.
It has the quality of breakup poetry, of getting over an ex and learning to let oneself love again. The poem previously appeared in an anthology, _Invisible Strings: 113 Poets Respond to the Songs of Taylor Swift_, which is perhaps telling of the tone, although I’m unsure of the way in which the poem responds to Taylor Swift. It may just be evocative of her style. Again, it doesn’t matter, for in romantic poetry the poem is primarily an emotional experience.
To express an emotion is not the same as understanding it: to understand it we must know and correctly judge its motive. I don’t know the motive behind Popa’s quest for healing and resolution because I don’t understand the circumstances of the relationship or the rift. This is intentional, part of her process of poetic composition. She desires only to suggest. This is fine for poems whose only aim is to evoke a mood, an atmosphere, a vibe, though it falls apart under the least scrutiny, in didactic poems like “Dark Matter” which lack scene and situation.
The injunction “You’d be a fool not to love until the last second” is evocative in the treacly way that Oliver’s most famous lines are. (“Tell me, what is it you plan to do
with your one wild and precious life?”) It gets the people going, as Will Ferrell says. But try and situate it within the context of the entire poem, and the sense doesn’t deepen but dissolve.

There’s dark matter, and then there’s desire that’s “the matter with our lives.” There is a logical progression from the first stanza to the second, where the first one sets up the vehicle of the metaphor and the second introduces its content, or tenor. We are to understand desire through its unknowability, then, like dark matter. Dark matter is a true mystery, and likewise the nature of desire is beyond our understanding, yet we can feel its effect on us. “Its command renews, swells and beckons.” Leaving aside the tenuousness of the metaphor itself (dark matter is hypothesized to exist, but its effect remains unobserved, least of all felt; gravity seems the better metaphor for something felt but not seen, but it’s also cliché) it’s the way Popa amplifies each part of the metaphor that confuses rather than elucidates their relationship. Dark matter is “a question that contends with the topsoil of time.” Desire is what’s the matter with our lives, the way a sea parts revealing another sea. These appositives are meant to amplify, but they also muddy the conceit. In what sense is a question contending with time a true mystery and not obfuscation? “Desire’s what’s the matter with our lives” is a clever transition, but in what sense is desire like a sea parting to reveal another sea like? How are we to take it in the context of what’s been said about dark matter? And why does it follow from desire’s command that “renews, swells and beckons” that we would be a fool not to love until the last second?

I know why these things sound good. The alliteration of “question contending” and “topsoil of time,” the slant rhyme of “beckons” and “second.” It’s got good ‘sonics’ (to use a much overused phrase in poetry today) but what is it saying? That despite its unknowability, we should give into desire’s journey. We’d be fools not to. The final line insists on its resolution as if it’s figured something out, as if it’s reasoned through the logic of its metaphors and arrived somewhere. In reality, the function of the imagery seems disjointed. The last line works as a slogan in isolation, in a picture frame or on a Dove chocolate wrapper, but not in the context of the poem, not as the conclusion to a line of reasoning which the poem would have us believe it’s getting at.
It’s easy enough to glide over this confusion, to skim the surface of the poem and feel oneself moved by the conviction and self-assurance of its tone. But inspect its rational content and the sense weakens. The confusion is one that gets at the heart of any romantic theory of poetry whereby reason is opposed and ultimately subordinated to feeling. For if a poem is purely an emotional experience, and the aim is self-expression, then reason can only get in the way, can only hinder the expression of that emotion. To think through it, to judge it correctly, is for the romantic poet to adulterate feeling. What the romantic poet seeks is to recreate their feeling as they felt it unmediated by the intellect.
This is what led Winters to conclude that the ideal poetic mode of production for the romantic is automatism. This mode was elaborated on explicitly by American romantic poets of the mid 20th century. Beat poets like Ginsberg and Kerouac, and Black Mountain poets like Charles Olson and Robert Creeley (who Popa cites as an influence in a recent interview) all had some theory of automatic writing which was, underneath, a romantic theory of composition.2 Such theories, although they’re no longer elucidated by our poets today, are nonetheless implicit in their work. In Popa it remains a noticeable and frustrating feature. She would have us believe that _If You Love That Lady_ gets to the bottom of desire and the stories we tell ourselves about desire, but the poems themselves never come off as wanting to understand their emotions, only feel them.

The flaw in this, as Winters pointed out, is that the emotional and rational content of a poem are inextricably linked. So long as language is the medium, the emotional content will be motivated to some degree by the poet’s rational considerations. To ignore or dismiss such considerations, or otherwise subordinate the rational to the emotional, makes for an inferior poem. To say that a poem has depth is the same thing as saying that the poet has considered the ways in which the rational content motivates and augments the emotional. But when the poet expresses their emotions without understanding, we as readers have no way of rightly judging them, but must simply take them as they come. It makes for less memorable poems, I think, less capable of deeply impressing in the memory or stirring the imagination which is both emotional and rational in nature.
For a general audience this is probably irrelevant. What matters, ultimately, is how a poem makes you feel. How did it strike you? What emotions did it make you feel? In this way we tend to consume poetry little differently than medication today, to alter moods and promote emotional well-being. I suspect Popa’s work will be well-received for this very reason. Like _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_, _If You Love That Lady_ leads the reader through loss and out the other side. Her poems evoke feelings that are generic enough that most will recognize something in them that they themselves have felt, even if they don’t understand exactly what’s being said. The ideas anyway are simple enough that they don’t really require explanation. Life is strange and wondrous. Desire is double-edged. Take deep breaths. Let go. Time heals all things. Such things go down easy as a pill. They can be read with ease, and are as easily dispensed with.
Despite his immense fame in his own time, William Cullen Bryant is now nearly forgotten. He disappeared in the shadow cast by Longfellow, a much better poet. I suspect, in time, something similar will happen to Mary Oliver. Her popularity will fade and seem, in a hundred years, curious and quaint. Her reputation will disappear in the shadow of a greater progeny writing in the major American style. But I’m not sure Maya Popa will be the one to cast that shadow. She remains a hopeless romantic.
1

During an online lecture/workshop I attended with the purchase of the book, Popa described the opening of “The Romantics” as both a way to avoid the use of an epigram to open the poem, and as an entrance into the writing of the poem. Popa believes that the excitement Keats expresses in the poem is the reason for his naming the wrong explorer, and this interpretation informs the emotional content of the rest of the poem. She avoids using a direct reference to the poem by mentioning a fact about its composition, although it seems a stretch to say that Keats named the wrong explorer intentionally because he was writing excitedly. The excitement is in the poem and not its composition.
2
For a previous post dealing with the difference between English and American romanticism, see here.

Dickens’ first question upon arriving in America was “Where is Bryant?” Edgar Allen Poe, too, wrote of Bryant with reverence. “In character no man stands more loftily… The peculiarly melancholy expression of his countenance has caused him to be accused of harshness, or coldness of heart. Never was there a greater mistake. His soul is charity itself, in all respects generous and noble.” Bryant went on walking tours abroad with Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Walter Savage Landor, and Robert and Elizabeth Browning. He knew James Fenimore Cooper, Fitz-Greene Halleck, and Thomas Cole. He was editor of the _New York Review_ and the _New York_ _Evening Post_. He edited the _Library of Poetry and Song_, a massive anthology of English and American verse. He was the first American to translate Homer. He advocated for international copyright protection. He even met with Andrew Jackson and advised Lincoln on cabinet appointments in 1861. He was, in short, an integral part of the culture. Above all, Bryant embodied the American man of letters and helped forge the American literary character. And it was to be a thoroughly romantic one.
His greatest poem, “Thanatopsis,” written when he was only 18, begins by introducing the essential Wordsworthian man
> To him who in the love of nature holds  
>   
> Communion with her visible forms, she speaks  
>   
> A various language
texts.3:
A meditation on death, Bryant urges us, when “thoughts of the last bitter hour come like a blight” on our spirits, to go into the woods and “list to Nature’s teachings.” Bryant’s narrators frequently implore us to escape into nature, or are escaping themselves. His subjects are the fairy music of green rivers, the solitude and splendor of winter woods, the summer wind, spring fountains, the heart-swelling vistas of prairies. His best poems are all variations on the theme of Nature’s restorative and instructive powers. He was hardly original in this, and the vividness of his descriptions are never as striking, nor his insights as deep or nuanced, as those of Wordsworth’s. But his career and work established in American poetry a voice that would carry through the transcendentalists down to Mary Oliver.
> My heart is awed within me, when I think  
>   
> Of the great miracle that still goes on,  
>   
> In silence, round me—the perpetual work  
>   
> Of thy creation, finished, yet renewed  
>   
> Forever. Written on thy works I read  
>   
> The lesson of thy own eternity.  
>   
> Lo! all grow old and die—but see, again,  
>   
> How on the faltering footsteps of decay  
>   
> Youth presses—ever gay and beautiful youth  
>   
> In all its beautiful forms. These lofty trees  
>   
> Wave not less proudly that their ancestors  
>   
> Moulder beneath them.  
>   
>   
> —from “Forest Hymn”
Oliver is as unoriginal as Bryant in this sense. Both preoccupied with nature and mortality and the relationship between them, both immensely popular because of their plain style and the simplicity of their ideas. Popa exists firmly within this tradition, and has since her previous book, _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ (Norton, 2022).
texts.4:
> The trees were on the verge of rebirth so sudden  
>   
> you’d miss it from one day to the next,  
>   
>   
> would be suddenly alive in it, the pale green bending open  
>   
> to reveal what we’d always suspected was the case:  
>   
>   
> that every bright thing has at its heart a hiddenness  
>   
> it offers when you’ve just about stopped looking.  
>   
>   
> from “All That Is Made”
Popa’s interest in the natural world is reparative, like Bryant’s. _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is about healing, whether from illness, the pandemic, death, loss. It’s about the ways in which suffering can open one up to feelings of awe. She tells us in “All Inner Life Runs At Some Delay” that “_Wound is where the light enters_,” a phrase she attributes to Rumi. Her new book, _If You Love That Lady_, is also about loss, the breaking off of a marriage that leaves the poet wandering in “the remainder of a life that love had made.”
The book’s title comes from a quote from Robert Graves’ advice to Siegfried Sassoon: “If you love that lady, don’t marry her.” It’s also the title of a collection of courtship letters between Sally McDowell and John Miller, which Popa tells us several of the poems were drawn from. McDowell was a 19th century Maryland socialite, the wife of the governor, who was accused by her jealous husband (who was 20 years her senior) of infidelity, and whose reputation was ruined by the accusations which the husband made public in a 52-page pamphlet which he distributed, incredibly, to all of Congress. McDowell was humiliated and ostracized. Afterwards she developed a relationship with John Miller, a Presbyterian minister, through a series of letters, and eventually the two married.
texts.5:
The letters show a woman struggling after public humiliation to let herself be loved again. The speaker in Popa’s collection, too, struggles to pick up the pieces of herself. She wanders through various cities and fragments of memories, with more ennui and with less focus than Popa’s previous effort, although with a familiar wound. The grief in _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is not unlike the heartbreak in _If You Love That Lady_. The basic presentation of suffering remains the same. It is elusive, elliptical, abstract. Always the hum of thoughts evaded by the mind. Familiar in the way it uses apostrophes addressed to “you,” in the way the unidentified pronouns fill the poems with a sense of intimacy. And although the presence of the natural world is somewhat diminished compared to _Wound_ (the style of _If You Love That Lady_ overall feels ‘diminished’) Popa continues to express a sensibility which is the inheritance of her romantic forbears. She embodies the American romantic in subject, sensibility, and in those theories that undergird romantic poetry.
The romantic theory prevalent in poetry operates under that assumption that literature is mainly or even purely an emotional experience. It often opposes the emotional to the rational, the emotional being ultimately good and desirable, while the rational is something to be looked on with suspicion. So in “The Conjunction of Jupiter and Venus,” William Cullen Bryant sets emotion and reason on the scale and weighs them against one another.
> I would not always reason. The straight path  
>   
> Wearies us with its never-varying lines,  
>   
> And we grow melancholy. I would make  
>   
> Reason my guide, but she should sometimes sit  
>   
> Patiently by the way-side, while I traced  
>   
> The mazes of the pleasant wilderness  
>   
> Around me. She should be my counsellor,  
>   
> But not my tyrant. For the spirit needs  
>   
> Impulses from a deeper source than hers,  
>   
> And there are motions, in the mind of man,  
>   
> That she must look upon with awe. I bow  
>   
> Reverently to her dictates, but not less  
>   
> Hold to the fair illusions of old time—  
>   
> Illusions that shed brightness over life,  
>   
> And glory over nature.
texts.6:
Bryant would make reason his guide, but he would not always follow its straight path, for there is something outside reason, beyond it. “Impulses from a deeper source than hers.” He calls them “Illusions that shed brightness over life, And glory over nature.” They are the source of life itself, invigorating and inspiring us. We experience them in moments of intense emotion. They are intuitive and irrational. One often encounters them in nature.
Mary Oliver describes something similar in “The Black Snake.” Upon finding a snake dead on the side of the road, struck by a driver, she pulls over to move its “looped and useless” body out of the way, and in the moment contemplates death
> its suddenness,  
>   
> its terrible weight,  
>   
> its certain coming. Yet under  
>   
>   
> reason burns a brighter fire, which the bones  
>   
> have always preferred.  
>   
> It is the story of endless good fortune.  
>   
> It says to oblivion: not me!  
>   
>   
> It is the light at the center of every cell.  
>   
> It is what sent the snake coiling and flowing forward  
>   
> happily all spring through the green leaves before  
>   
> he came to the road.
Oliver, like Bryant, opposes this animating force to reason. It is underneath reason and “burns a brighter fire, which the bones have always preferred.” She encounters it, like Bryant, in nature. The road, meanwhile, which is manmade, is unnatural. It is part of the ordered world of civilization. It is what killed the snake who, before it slithered out onto it, was “coiling and flowing forward happily all spring.” It is the same straight path of reason which Bryant, in his poem, would not always follow. So both poets maintain an essentially romantic outlook which identifies the good with feeling and nature, the bad with reason and civilization.
Whereas Bryant is skeptical of reason, recognizing its limitations, yet practical in his desire to join it with feeling, Oliver is more dismissive of reason. She has no use for it. In “What is There Beyond Knowing” she tells us
texts.14:
It is an understanding which does not seek to understand, but to simply be, to exist, without thinking. It is a call to slow down and breathe. Simple and plain. As the poem which begins the third and final section, “The World” marks a transition in the narrative arc of _If You Love That Lady_ that will conclude with the final lines of “It All Comes Back To Me Now,” lines that lift and make light of that weight of grief the poet has been carrying throughout:
> Here I am, filled out by happiness  
>   
> I could not otherwise have earned.  
>   
>   
> God forbid I hadn’t taken every last wrong turn.
It has the quality of breakup poetry, of getting over an ex and learning to let oneself love again. The poem previously appeared in an anthology, _Invisible Strings: 113 Poets Respond to the Songs of Taylor Swift_, which is perhaps telling of the tone, although I’m unsure of the way in which the poem responds to Taylor Swift. It may just be evocative of her style. Again, it doesn’t matter, for in romantic poetry the poem is primarily an emotional experience.
To express an emotion is not the same as understanding it: to understand it we must know and correctly judge its motive. I don’t know the motive behind Popa’s quest for healing and resolution because I don’t understand the circumstances of the relationship or the rift. This is intentional, part of her process of poetic composition. She desires only to suggest. This is fine for poems whose only aim is to evoke a mood, an atmosphere, a vibe, though it falls apart under the least scrutiny, in didactic poems like “Dark Matter” which lack scene and situation.
The injunction “You’d be a fool not to love until the last second” is evocative in the treacly way that Oliver’s most famous lines are. (“Tell me, what is it you plan to do
with your one wild and precious life?”) It gets the people going, as Will Ferrell says. But try and situate it within the context of the entire poem, and the sense doesn’t deepen but dissolve.
texts.15: There’s dark matter, and then there’s desire that’s “the matter with our lives.” There is a logical progression from the first stanza to the second, where the first one sets up the vehicle of the metaphor and the second introduces its content, or tenor. We are to understand desire through its unknowability, then, like dark matter. Dark matter is a true mystery, and likewise the nature of desire is beyond our understanding, yet we can feel its effect on us. “Its command renews, swells and beckons.” Leaving aside the tenuousness of the metaphor itself (dark matter is hypothesized to exist, but its effect remains unobserved, least of all felt; gravity seems the better metaphor for something felt but not seen, but it’s also cliché) it’s the way Popa amplifies each part of the metaphor that confuses rather than elucidates their relationship. Dark matter is “a question that contends with the topsoil of time.” Desire is what’s the matter with our lives, the way a sea parts revealing another sea. These appositives are meant to amplify, but they also muddy the conceit. In what sense is a question contending with time a true mystery and not obfuscation? “Desire’s what’s the matter with our lives” is a clever transition, but in what sense is desire like a sea parting to reveal another sea like? How are we to take it in the context of what’s been said about dark matter? And why does it follow from desire’s command that “renews, swells and beckons” that we would be a fool not to love until the last second?
texts.16:
I know why these things sound good. The alliteration of “question contending” and “topsoil of time,” the slant rhyme of “beckons” and “second.” It’s got good ‘sonics’ (to use a much overused phrase in poetry today) but what is it saying? That despite its unknowability, we should give into desire’s journey. We’d be fools not to. The final line insists on its resolution as if it’s figured something out, as if it’s reasoned through the logic of its metaphors and arrived somewhere. In reality, the function of the imagery seems disjointed. The last line works as a slogan in isolation, in a picture frame or on a Dove chocolate wrapper, but not in the context of the poem, not as the conclusion to a line of reasoning which the poem would have us believe it’s getting at.
It’s easy enough to glide over this confusion, to skim the surface of the poem and feel oneself moved by the conviction and self-assurance of its tone. But inspect its rational content and the sense weakens. The confusion is one that gets at the heart of any romantic theory of poetry whereby reason is opposed and ultimately subordinated to feeling. For if a poem is purely an emotional experience, and the aim is self-expression, then reason can only get in the way, can only hinder the expression of that emotion. To think through it, to judge it correctly, is for the romantic poet to adulterate feeling. What the romantic poet seeks is to recreate their feeling as they felt it unmediated by the intellect.
This is what led Winters to conclude that the ideal poetic mode of production for the romantic is automatism. This mode was elaborated on explicitly by American romantic poets of the mid 20th century. Beat poets like Ginsberg and Kerouac, and Black Mountain poets like Charles Olson and Robert Creeley (who Popa cites as an influence in a recent interview) all had some theory of automatic writing which was, underneath, a romantic theory of composition.2 Such theories, although they’re no longer elucidated by our poets today, are nonetheless implicit in their work. In Popa it remains a noticeable and frustrating feature. She would have us believe that _If You Love That Lady_ gets to the bottom of desire and the stories we tell ourselves about desire, but the poems themselves never come off as wanting to understand their emotions, only feel them.
texts.17:
The flaw in this, as Winters pointed out, is that the emotional and rational content of a poem are inextricably linked. So long as language is the medium, the emotional content will be motivated to some degree by the poet’s rational considerations. To ignore or dismiss such considerations, or otherwise subordinate the rational to the emotional, makes for an inferior poem. To say that a poem has depth is the same thing as saying that the poet has considered the ways in which the rational content motivates and augments the emotional. But when the poet expresses their emotions without understanding, we as readers have no way of rightly judging them, but must simply take them as they come. It makes for less memorable poems, I think, less capable of deeply impressing in the memory or stirring the imagination which is both emotional and rational in nature.
For a general audience this is probably irrelevant. What matters, ultimately, is how a poem makes you feel. How did it strike you? What emotions did it make you feel? In this way we tend to consume poetry little differently than medication today, to alter moods and promote emotional well-being. I suspect Popa’s work will be well-received for this very reason. Like _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_, _If You Love That Lady_ leads the reader through loss and out the other side. Her poems evoke feelings that are generic enough that most will recognize something in them that they themselves have felt, even if they don’t understand exactly what’s being said. The ideas anyway are simple enough that they don’t really require explanation. Life is strange and wondrous. Desire is double-edged. Take deep breaths. Let go. Time heals all things. Such things go down easy as a pill. They can be read with ease, and are as easily dispensed with.
Despite his immense fame in his own time, William Cullen Bryant is now nearly forgotten. He disappeared in the shadow cast by Longfellow, a much better poet. I suspect, in time, something similar will happen to Mary Oliver. Her popularity will fade and seem, in a hundred years, curious and quaint. Her reputation will disappear in the shadow of a greater progeny writing in the major American style. But I’m not sure Maya Popa will be the one to cast that shadow. She remains a hopeless romantic.
1
texts.18:
During an online lecture/workshop I attended with the purchase of the book, Popa described the opening of “The Romantics” as both a way to avoid the use of an epigram to open the poem, and as an entrance into the writing of the poem. Popa believes that the excitement Keats expresses in the poem is the reason for his naming the wrong explorer, and this interpretation informs the emotional content of the rest of the poem. She avoids using a direct reference to the poem by mentioning a fact about its composition, although it seems a stretch to say that Keats named the wrong explorer intentionally because he was writing excitedly. The excitement is in the poem and not its composition.
