Title: Maya Popa is a Hopeless Romantic
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,14,15,16,17,18
What is the major voice in American poetry today? What is the popular style? What is that generic contemporary idiom such that, if one would hear with the ears closed, picturing with the aural imagination, they would hear its tone of voice? What would such a voice sound like, and what would it suggest? What would we hear in its pitch and stress, in its timbre, in the manner of its cadences and in the arguments of its melodies?
Robert Frost called such hearing the sound of sense. “The abstract vitality of our speech.” It’s what we can intuit from conversations overheard from behind a wall or across a café. The tunes one remembers without remembering all the words.
If you squinted at contemporary poetry with your ears, you might at first audially imagine many different styles. The softspokenness of an academic, the rhythm of a spoken word poet at an open mic, the earnestness of a teenager in front of a phone screen. Whatever you imagined, the generic voice would probably sound a bit like all of these. It would sound, as with all poetry, elevated in manner from regular speech. Its language would be ostentatious, suggesting more than in prose. Conversational, plainspoken, yet lyrical. It would speak with candor about the personal, yet it would be highly impressionistic and self-conscious. It would be written in free verse, and it would not rhyme, but it would be ‘sonic.’ It would aim at self-expression and powerful feeling above all else. Its character would be essentially romantic, as the major American mode has always been.
I imagine, above all, someone like Mary Oliver. Popular since the 80s, she remains beloved and imitated. Her influence can be felt from academia to Instagram. Her expressions permeate the popular culture. A new documentary out this year about her life, _Saved by the Beauty of the World,_ positions Oliver as the poet who’s read by people who don’t like poetry. It features celebrity champions of poetry like Helena Bonham Carter, Stephen Colbert, and Oprah Winfrey. Oliver is undoubtedly a conduit of the tradition. Her style draws from many strands, making something homogeneous and mainstream. Her writing is accessible and her sentiments about nature and beauty seem quintessential to poetry. Generically beautiful, intimate, poignant, feminine, romantic.

If I had to picture which voice most closely resembles that style today, I would picture Maya Popa. I would hear in my mind’s ear Maya Popa’s voice. She is, I think, an heir to Mary Oliver, perhaps _the_ heir, and her newest collection, _If You Love That Lady_ (Norton), sounds like the major American idiom of the last few decades.
Though she does not have the popularity of Kaur or Gorman or Vuong, Popa has nevertheless achieved success in the poetry world. She is published by Norton, and regularly appears in major trad magazines like _The New Yorker_, _The Atlantic_, and _The Guardian_. She’s an editor for _Publisher’s Weekly_. She’s escaped the confines of academia and MFA programs (though she is the product of an MFA from NYU) and found mainstream success through Substack (22,000+ subscribers) and the Conscious Writers Collective. Her website says she’s been commissioned by major institutions including the United Nations, the Grotte de Lazaret, and Van Cleef & Arpels. She has a broad reading audience beyond poets themselves, and is popular for the same reasons as Oliver: her style is accessible, and her message, whether of enchantment, desire, or mortality, is a simple and perennial one.
Maya Popa is part of the American romantic tradition that has been the dominant poetic voice in the country since its founding. Indeed, American poetry has always been the child of the English Romantics. We had our Augustan imitators, poets of the Revolution like Freneau and the Connecticut Wits, but in the first decades after independence, when America was still in its infancy, still forming its identity, English Romanticism was ascendant. American poets adopted the style because it was fashionable, but also because its spirit was really our spirit. Born of radical Enlightenment principles, but democratic and less sophisticated than our European counterparts, we naturally preferred self-reliance and instinct over reason. Protestantism taught us to listen to our hearts and trust our intuitions, and the natural world, the Frontier, was an ever-present part of the American condition. This was the place for the Romanticism, and so the style of Pope naturally gave way to the style of Wordsworth. We traded neoclassicism for naturalism, and heroic couplets for blank verse.

Our first popular poet, William Cullen Bryant was a self-acknowledged student of Wordsworth. Now mostly forgotten, he was in his time a sensation, as renowned as Charles Dickens, who he entertained on a visit to New York in 1842. Dickens’ first question upon arriving in America was “Where is Bryant?” Edgar Allen Poe, too, wrote of Bryant with reverence. “In character no man stands more loftily… The peculiarly melancholy expression of his countenance has caused him to be accused of harshness, or coldness of heart. Never was there a greater mistake. His soul is charity itself, in all respects generous and noble.” Bryant went on walking tours abroad with Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Walter Savage Landor, and Robert and Elizabeth Browning. He knew James Fenimore Cooper, Fitz-Greene Halleck, and Thomas Cole. He was editor of the _New York Review_ and the _New York_ _Evening Post_. He edited the _Library of Poetry and Song_, a massive anthology of English and American verse. He was the first American to translate Homer. He advocated for international copyright protection. He even met with Andrew Jackson and advised Lincoln on cabinet appointments in 1861. He was, in short, an integral part of the culture. Above all, Bryant embodied the American man of letters and helped forge the American literary character. And it was to be a thoroughly romantic one.
His greatest poem, “Thanatopsis,” written when he was only 18, begins by introducing the essential Wordsworthian man
> To him who in the love of nature holds  
>   
> Communion with her visible forms, she speaks  
>   
> A various language

A meditation on death, Bryant urges us, when “thoughts of the last bitter hour come like a blight” on our spirits, to go into the woods and “list to Nature’s teachings.” Bryant’s narrators frequently implore us to escape into nature, or are escaping themselves. His subjects are the fairy music of green rivers, the solitude and splendor of winter woods, the summer wind, spring fountains, the heart-swelling vistas of prairies. His best poems are all variations on the theme of Nature’s restorative and instructive powers. He was hardly original in this, and the vividness of his descriptions are never as striking, nor his insights as deep or nuanced, as those of Wordsworth’s. But his career and work established in American poetry a voice that would carry through the transcendentalists down to Mary Oliver.
> My heart is awed within me, when I think  
>   
> Of the great miracle that still goes on,  
>   
> In silence, round me—the perpetual work  
>   
> Of thy creation, finished, yet renewed  
>   
> Forever. Written on thy works I read  
>   
> The lesson of thy own eternity.  
>   
> Lo! all grow old and die—but see, again,  
>   
> How on the faltering footsteps of decay  
>   
> Youth presses—ever gay and beautiful youth  
>   
> In all its beautiful forms. These lofty trees  
>   
> Wave not less proudly that their ancestors  
>   
> Moulder beneath them.  
>   
>   
> —from “Forest Hymn”
Oliver is as unoriginal as Bryant in this sense. Both preoccupied with nature and mortality and the relationship between them, both immensely popular because of their plain style and the simplicity of their ideas. Popa exists firmly within this tradition, and has since her previous book, _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ (Norton, 2022).

> The trees were on the verge of rebirth so sudden  
>   
> you’d miss it from one day to the next,  
>   
>   
> would be suddenly alive in it, the pale green bending open  
>   
> to reveal what we’d always suspected was the case:  
>   
>   
> that every bright thing has at its heart a hiddenness  
>   
> it offers when you’ve just about stopped looking.  
>   
>   
> from “All That Is Made”
Popa’s interest in the natural world is reparative, like Bryant’s. _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is about healing, whether from illness, the pandemic, death, loss. It’s about the ways in which suffering can open one up to feelings of awe. She tells us in “All Inner Life Runs At Some Delay” that “_Wound is where the light enters_,” a phrase she attributes to Rumi. Her new book, _If You Love That Lady_, is also about loss, the breaking off of a marriage that leaves the poet wandering in “the remainder of a life that love had made.”
The book’s title comes from a quote from Robert Graves’ advice to Siegfried Sassoon: “If you love that lady, don’t marry her.” It’s also the title of a collection of courtship letters between Sally McDowell and John Miller, which Popa tells us several of the poems were drawn from. McDowell was a 19th century Maryland socialite, the wife of the governor, who was accused by her jealous husband (who was 20 years her senior) of infidelity, and whose reputation was ruined by the accusations which the husband made public in a 52-page pamphlet which he distributed, incredibly, to all of Congress. McDowell was humiliated and ostracized. Afterwards she developed a relationship with John Miller, a Presbyterian minister, through a series of letters, and eventually the two married.

The letters show a woman struggling after public humiliation to let herself be loved again. The speaker in Popa’s collection, too, struggles to pick up the pieces of herself. She wanders through various cities and fragments of memories, with more ennui and with less focus than Popa’s previous effort, although with a familiar wound. The grief in _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_ is not unlike the heartbreak in _If You Love That Lady_. The basic presentation of suffering remains the same. It is elusive, elliptical, abstract. Always the hum of thoughts evaded by the mind. Familiar in the way it uses apostrophes addressed to “you,” in the way the unidentified pronouns fill the poems with a sense of intimacy. And although the presence of the natural world is somewhat diminished compared to _Wound_ (the style of _If You Love That Lady_ overall feels ‘diminished’) Popa continues to express a sensibility which is the inheritance of her romantic forbears. She embodies the American romantic in subject, sensibility, and in those theories that undergird romantic poetry.
The romantic theory prevalent in poetry operates under that assumption that literature is mainly or even purely an emotional experience. It often opposes the emotional to the rational, the emotional being ultimately good and desirable, while the rational is something to be looked on with suspicion. So in “The Conjunction of Jupiter and Venus,” William Cullen Bryant sets emotion and reason on the scale and weighs them against one another.
> I would not always reason. The straight path  
>   
> Wearies us with its never-varying lines,  
>   
> And we grow melancholy. I would make  
>   
> Reason my guide, but she should sometimes sit  
>   
> Patiently by the way-side, while I traced  
>   
> The mazes of the pleasant wilderness  
>   
> Around me. She should be my counsellor,  
>   
> But not my tyrant. For the spirit needs  
>   
> Impulses from a deeper source than hers,  
>   
> And there are motions, in the mind of man,  
>   
> That she must look upon with awe. I bow  
>   
> Reverently to her dictates, but not less  
>   
> Hold to the fair illusions of old time—  
>   
> Illusions that shed brightness over life,  
>   
> And glory over nature.

Bryant would make reason his guide, but he would not always follow its straight path, for there is something outside reason, beyond it. “Impulses from a deeper source than hers.” He calls them “Illusions that shed brightness over life, And glory over nature.” They are the source of life itself, invigorating and inspiring us. We experience them in moments of intense emotion. They are intuitive and irrational. One often encounters them in nature.
Mary Oliver describes something similar in “The Black Snake.” Upon finding a snake dead on the side of the road, struck by a driver, she pulls over to move its “looped and useless” body out of the way, and in the moment contemplates death
> its suddenness,  
>   
> its terrible weight,  
>   
> its certain coming. Yet under  
>   
>   
> reason burns a brighter fire, which the bones  
>   
> have always preferred.  
>   
> It is the story of endless good fortune.  
>   
> It says to oblivion: not me!  
>   
>   
> It is the light at the center of every cell.  
>   
> It is what sent the snake coiling and flowing forward  
>   
> happily all spring through the green leaves before  
>   
> he came to the road.
Oliver, like Bryant, opposes this animating force to reason. It is underneath reason and “burns a brighter fire, which the bones have always preferred.” She encounters it, like Bryant, in nature. The road, meanwhile, which is manmade, is unnatural. It is part of the ordered world of civilization. It is what killed the snake who, before it slithered out onto it, was “coiling and flowing forward happily all spring.” It is the same straight path of reason which Bryant, in his poem, would not always follow. So both poets maintain an essentially romantic outlook which identifies the good with feeling and nature, the bad with reason and civilization.
Whereas Bryant is skeptical of reason, recognizing its limitations, yet practical in his desire to join it with feeling, Oliver is more dismissive of reason. She has no use for it. In “What is There Beyond Knowing” she tells us

It is an understanding which does not seek to understand, but to simply be, to exist, without thinking. It is a call to slow down and breathe. Simple and plain. As the poem which begins the third and final section, “The World” marks a transition in the narrative arc of _If You Love That Lady_ that will conclude with the final lines of “It All Comes Back To Me Now,” lines that lift and make light of that weight of grief the poet has been carrying throughout:
> Here I am, filled out by happiness  
>   
> I could not otherwise have earned.  
>   
>   
> God forbid I hadn’t taken every last wrong turn.
It has the quality of breakup poetry, of getting over an ex and learning to let oneself love again. The poem previously appeared in an anthology, _Invisible Strings: 113 Poets Respond to the Songs of Taylor Swift_, which is perhaps telling of the tone, although I’m unsure of the way in which the poem responds to Taylor Swift. It may just be evocative of her style. Again, it doesn’t matter, for in romantic poetry the poem is primarily an emotional experience.
To express an emotion is not the same as understanding it: to understand it we must know and correctly judge its motive. I don’t know the motive behind Popa’s quest for healing and resolution because I don’t understand the circumstances of the relationship or the rift. This is intentional, part of her process of poetic composition. She desires only to suggest. This is fine for poems whose only aim is to evoke a mood, an atmosphere, a vibe, though it falls apart under the least scrutiny, in didactic poems like “Dark Matter” which lack scene and situation.
The injunction “You’d be a fool not to love until the last second” is evocative in the treacly way that Oliver’s most famous lines are. (“Tell me, what is it you plan to do
with your one wild and precious life?”) It gets the people going, as Will Ferrell says. But try and situate it within the context of the entire poem, and the sense doesn’t deepen but dissolve.

There’s dark matter, and then there’s desire that’s “the matter with our lives.” There is a logical progression from the first stanza to the second, where the first one sets up the vehicle of the metaphor and the second introduces its content, or tenor. We are to understand desire through its unknowability, then, like dark matter. Dark matter is a true mystery, and likewise the nature of desire is beyond our understanding, yet we can feel its effect on us. “Its command renews, swells and beckons.” Leaving aside the tenuousness of the metaphor itself (dark matter is hypothesized to exist, but its effect remains unobserved, least of all felt; gravity seems the better metaphor for something felt but not seen, but it’s also cliché) it’s the way Popa amplifies each part of the metaphor that confuses rather than elucidates their relationship. Dark matter is “a question that contends with the topsoil of time.” Desire is what’s the matter with our lives, the way a sea parts revealing another sea. These appositives are meant to amplify, but they also muddy the conceit. In what sense is a question contending with time a true mystery and not obfuscation? “Desire’s what’s the matter with our lives” is a clever transition, but in what sense is desire like a sea parting to reveal another sea like? How are we to take it in the context of what’s been said about dark matter? And why does it follow from desire’s command that “renews, swells and beckons” that we would be a fool not to love until the last second?

I know why these things sound good. The alliteration of “question contending” and “topsoil of time,” the slant rhyme of “beckons” and “second.” It’s got good ‘sonics’ (to use a much overused phrase in poetry today) but what is it saying? That despite its unknowability, we should give into desire’s journey. We’d be fools not to. The final line insists on its resolution as if it’s figured something out, as if it’s reasoned through the logic of its metaphors and arrived somewhere. In reality, the function of the imagery seems disjointed. The last line works as a slogan in isolation, in a picture frame or on a Dove chocolate wrapper, but not in the context of the poem, not as the conclusion to a line of reasoning which the poem would have us believe it’s getting at.
It’s easy enough to glide over this confusion, to skim the surface of the poem and feel oneself moved by the conviction and self-assurance of its tone. But inspect its rational content and the sense weakens. The confusion is one that gets at the heart of any romantic theory of poetry whereby reason is opposed and ultimately subordinated to feeling. For if a poem is purely an emotional experience, and the aim is self-expression, then reason can only get in the way, can only hinder the expression of that emotion. To think through it, to judge it correctly, is for the romantic poet to adulterate feeling. What the romantic poet seeks is to recreate their feeling as they felt it unmediated by the intellect.
This is what led Winters to conclude that the ideal poetic mode of production for the romantic is automatism. This mode was elaborated on explicitly by American romantic poets of the mid 20th century. Beat poets like Ginsberg and Kerouac, and Black Mountain poets like Charles Olson and Robert Creeley (who Popa cites as an influence in a recent interview) all had some theory of automatic writing which was, underneath, a romantic theory of composition.2 Such theories, although they’re no longer elucidated by our poets today, are nonetheless implicit in their work. In Popa it remains a noticeable and frustrating feature. She would have us believe that _If You Love That Lady_ gets to the bottom of desire and the stories we tell ourselves about desire, but the poems themselves never come off as wanting to understand their emotions, only feel them.

The flaw in this, as Winters pointed out, is that the emotional and rational content of a poem are inextricably linked. So long as language is the medium, the emotional content will be motivated to some degree by the poet’s rational considerations. To ignore or dismiss such considerations, or otherwise subordinate the rational to the emotional, makes for an inferior poem. To say that a poem has depth is the same thing as saying that the poet has considered the ways in which the rational content motivates and augments the emotional. But when the poet expresses their emotions without understanding, we as readers have no way of rightly judging them, but must simply take them as they come. It makes for less memorable poems, I think, less capable of deeply impressing in the memory or stirring the imagination which is both emotional and rational in nature.
For a general audience this is probably irrelevant. What matters, ultimately, is how a poem makes you feel. How did it strike you? What emotions did it make you feel? In this way we tend to consume poetry little differently than medication today, to alter moods and promote emotional well-being. I suspect Popa’s work will be well-received for this very reason. Like _Wound is the Origin of Wonder_, _If You Love That Lady_ leads the reader through loss and out the other side. Her poems evoke feelings that are generic enough that most will recognize something in them that they themselves have felt, even if they don’t understand exactly what’s being said. The ideas anyway are simple enough that they don’t really require explanation. Life is strange and wondrous. Desire is double-edged. Take deep breaths. Let go. Time heals all things. Such things go down easy as a pill. They can be read with ease, and are as easily dispensed with.
Despite his immense fame in his own time, William Cullen Bryant is now nearly forgotten. He disappeared in the shadow cast by Longfellow, a much better poet. I suspect, in time, something similar will happen to Mary Oliver. Her popularity will fade and seem, in a hundred years, curious and quaint. Her reputation will disappear in the shadow of a greater progeny writing in the major American style. But I’m not sure Maya Popa will be the one to cast that shadow. She remains a hopeless romantic.

During an online lecture/workshop I attended with the purchase of the book, Popa described the opening of “The Romantics” as both a way to avoid the use of an epigram to open the poem, and as an entrance into the writing of the poem. Popa believes that the excitement Keats expresses in the poem is the reason for his naming the wrong explorer, and this interpretation informs the emotional content of the rest of the poem. She avoids using a direct reference to the poem by mentioning a fact about its composition, although it seems a stretch to say that Keats named the wrong explorer intentionally because he was writing excitedly. The excitement is in the poem and not its composition.

Title: “Poetry has great work to do”: An Interview with Carolyn Forché
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
One day when Carolyn Forché was in her twenties, a man she had never met arrived at her house with two young girls, a beat-up truck, and pages of documents concerning the history of the US government and El Salvador. This man, Leonel Gómez Vides, would alter the course of Forché’s life. In her recent memoir, _What You Have Heard Is True—_ her first published work of prose—Forché recounts the experiences that this meeting led her to witness in El Salvador in the late 1970s, just before the country was consumed by civil war.
When Leonel Gómez arrived at Forché’s door, she was living a studious life in southern California, teaching writing at a university. She had previously spent a summer in Mallorca translating the work of Nicaraguan-Salvadoran poet Claribel Alegría, whose daughter was a friend of Forché’s. Alegría had mentioned Forché’s work to Gómez, who decided he needed someone from the US to witness what was happening in El Salvador and decided to find this poet. This lead to the first of many visits Forché made to El Salvador between 1978 and 1980. While she wrote some articles about her time there, the poems in her 1981 collection, _The Country Between Us_, relate the violence and the normalization of cruelty that she witnessed in obliquely crushing, brutal language.
_What You Have Heard Is True_ recounts the people and situations Forché encountered in towns, neighborhoods, mountain villages, and rural hospitals all over the country; Gómez takes her along with him as he talks with everyone from farmers to military officers, ambassadors to informants. As the violence intensifies, she relies on excerpts pulled from her notebooks at the time to capture the imagery, sensations, and palpable tension—perhaps most apparent in what goes unsaid. Some of these images are echoed in the language of her poems on El Salvador, such as those in _The Colonel._

In 1993, Forché edited an anthology of poems, _Against Forgetting: Twentieth-Century Poetry of Witness_, which brought together her interests in human rights and poetry _._ The 145 works in the collection come from poets around the world who had “endured conditions of historical and social extremity during the twentieth century.” These poems were to be read within the context of a term that Forché coined in the collection’s introduction, “poetry of witness.”
Poetry of witness is not political or partisan, it is a testament to the truth. It is a witnessing of violence and a documentation of the human reaction to this violence. Forché writes in the introduction to this anthology that “these poems bear a trace of extremity within them, and they are, as such, evidence of what occurred.”
I recently spoke with Forché about the distinct ways in which journalism and poetry interact with violence and how each can be utilized to record acts against humanity—as a form of witness.
**Claire Mullen: In _What You Have Heard Is True,_ you delve into the complicated relationship between writing and personal experience. In journalism, it is antithetical to include your own experience in a story because it can indicate bias, whereas poems are often about the very personal. How do you think about the delineation between journalism and poetry in response to violence, and what was your experience with this in El Salvador?**
**Carolyn Forché:** Back then, I wrote for the _Nation_, the _Progressive_, and others, but I very happily abandoned that. I am not a journalist or a historian. I was rather free to be a literary writer and a poet and to write about my own experience because I wasn’t constricted by journalistic conventions.
There’s a frustration for journalists that they can’t speak about their experiences easily in their reporting. What I’ve noticed is that many journalists do their reporting, and then they will write a memoir or nonfiction book about their experience. For example, the great wonderful woman photographer Jean-Marie Simon who photographed throughout the War in Guatemala, and also the genocide in Guatemala, is now working on a memoir about her own experience. One of the most impressive journalists of the twentieth century, the Polish journalist Ryszard Kapuscinski, drew a line between his reporting and his own investigation of the world, as he put it, “on foot.”

These people have been great models for me, and it corresponds in some ways to the division between my poetry and this memoir. In the nonfiction memoir, I’m actually telling a story, and I’m trying to shape that story and structure it. I hadn’t written prose for years, and it was a challenge for me. It’s a different mind. We write from within a different consciousness when we’re writing nonfiction prose and poetry. When I’m writing poetry, I work with the associational mind; I’m not always completely conscious of what I’m doing. I would say that is less so when I was writing the nonfiction book because that was a retrieval from memory.
**CM: In the memoir, you include sections which seem to be excerpts from your notebooks from the time you were in El Salvador, and the writing verges on stream of consciousness. Some of these excerpts include sketches of ideas or imagery that are echoed in poems in _The Country Between Us._ Could you describe your writing process and how these excerpts relate to your finished poems?**
**CF:**In my adulthood as a poet, I’ve always carried small notebooks with me wherever I’ve gone. I don’t chronicle my life in them, I simply write down things as I think of them. Sometimes it’ll be a line, or a list of words, or an image that I see and I take a note of it. I’m very interested in the fact that a lot of poets that I have researched, living and dead, also kept such notebooks. It seems to be a pattern with poets.
When I was in El Salvador, I wasn’t writing poetry very much. There are only seven poems in _The Country Between Us_ that have to do with El Salvador, and most of them were written during periods when I was back in the United States. It was very intense there. There was a great deal of fear in the air, and that isn’t conducive to writing poetry. I was writing as fast as I could just to get things down before they drifted away and when I had the peace of mind or clarity to write them. They were my escape, so there are these many, many notebooks, and those passages came from them.

One thing that I’ve noticed is that very often when I’m writing a poem, I have the feeling that I’ve written it before. When I go back to the notebooks, I often find the vocabulary of the poem or several lines that indeed I did write before. So the seeds of the first drafts are often in the notebooks. Again, not recording my life events, but rather whatever comes from my consciousness.
**CM: Is this what you would describe as the associational thinking that you experience when writing poetry?**
**CF:**Yes. Sometimes it’ll take shape and sometimes it’s all fragmented. It’s a useful practice because it allows me to maintain the connection between the pen and the mind so that I can be surprised by what happens and make discoveries through the language itself, rather than pre-conceiving what I want to say or write. I don’t think that poetry at its best comes from preconceived message or ideas. It’s not intentional in that way.
Learning to write the memoir was a process in itself. I wrote more as a poet writes, polishing every sentence. I had a difficult time moving forward, and I also had a difficult time learning how to focus on one slice of my life. A memoir is not an autobiography, so there are many parts of life that have to be left out or just skipped over, because what you’re trying to do is tell a story that may move through time.
Also, I decided that I wanted the reader not to know more than what I knew at the time. I tried to take the reader with me on the journey that I took. I wanted to see if I could replicate it. Rather than have extensive retrospection and analysis throughout, I allowed the story to unfold without interference. Once I made that decision, I also made the discovery that inserting the excerpted passages would help me to tell the story as it happened. I could include them and it would add a dimension of a different kind of language, the kind of writing that happens under stress, and under trauma, and it’s very different, as you noticed.
**CM: Throughout the memoir, it is clear that you as a narrator are learning, you’re growing and becoming someone else. It’s fascinating that that was a deliberate choice on your part to make the reader learn along with the narrator.**
**CF:**Well, thank you. What I wanted to do was to write a transformative memoir.

Title: Sharon Olds
Chunks: 0,1,2
### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
Photo by Catherine Mauger
**Sharon Olds** was born in San Francisco and studied at Stanford University and Columbia University. When her first book was published, she was a few years shy of 40. Within a decade, she’d become the director of the Graduate Writing Program at NYU and released several highly acclaimed, best-selling collections. Her books include _Satan Says_ (1980), _The Dead and the Living_ (1984), _The Gold Cell_ (1987), _The Matter of This World_ (1987), _The Sign of Saturn_ (1991), _The Father_ (1992), _The Wellspring_ (1996), _Blood, Tin, Straw_ (1999), _The Unswept Room_ (2002), _Strike Sparks_ (2004), and _One Secret Thing_ (2008). Her poems have also appeared in more than 100 poetry anthologies.   
Olds was poet laureate of New York from 1998 to 2000. Her many honors include the T.S. Eliot Prize, the National Book Critics Circle Award, and the Pulitzer Prize. Her most recent collection, _Stag’s Leap_, came out in 2012.
**What started you writing poetry?**
I started writing poems as a child and teenager. I think what made me start was the desire to “sing,” to make up word songs, to play with words and rhymes, to tell a story.
**Your collection _Stag’s Leap_ won both the T.S Eliot Prize and the Pulitzer Prize last year. These intimate poems chronicle the dissolution of a marriage of 32 years after the husband abruptly leaves his wife for another woman. Can you speak about the title? _Stag’s Leap_ evokes such exuberance and vitality in contrast with the many painful images throughout the book.**

### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
The title poem is named after a wine, in fact after a wine label, which has a picture of a leaping deer on it. The poem is a portrait of a departing or escaping creature. I’m glad if it has vitality! I guess my hope would be that the images in the book, painful or not, would have their own vitality and give the reader pleasure.
**What was the process like assembling the poems as a whole?**
First I assembled all the poems I’d written on the subject, over 10 years, which I’d liked well enough to type up and revise. (Which was a fraction of the number I’d written on the subject.) Then I tried to narrow the group down to what I thought were the best of them, and then I looked for how they seemed to organize themselves. I did this on the dining room floor! Changing the order over and over until it seemed right.
**When people describe your work, they inevitably talk about its autobiographical aspects. In fact, _Stag’s Leap_ can be found under “Biographies and Memoirs” on Amazon, which seems unusual for a book of poetry. Do you mind being considered a distinctly autobiographical poet?**
What interests me most about the poems I read (and write) are things like the images, the music (rhyme and meter), and how the sentence and the line interconnect with each other in the poem. Over the years, I haven’t talked much about biographies and memoirs — though I love reading them; what has interested me most about poems is the art of them — what each one is doing, and how.
**You’ve said that you want a poem to be useful above all else. Can you talk about this a bit more?**
I think the arts exist because they are useful — essential to our species. I think it’s part of being human, to make art and need art. For the pleasure of it, and for whatever knowledge we get out of it. Reading each other helps us imagine each other. And empathy seems like something we are in great need of, as a species, in order to survive.
**Although your work is commonly described as free verse, you’ve mentioned that your next book will concentrate on odes. Is it liberating or particularly challenging to work in a more formal structure?**

### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
I have not, over the years, tried to write in a particular form, but when I look at my poems, I see that they have been written in four-beat lines (four strong accents, however many syllables the line has), with few end-stopped lines, and a lot of enjambment (the sentence pouring over the end of one line into the next). So I see myself as a formal poet: four-beat lines, and enjambment, and internal — rather than end-stopped — rhyme being my form. (I don’t see myself as writing “free verse.”)
As for the odes I’ve been writing, they may not be odes at all — I’ve been afraid to look up _ode_ in case it’s an illusion of mind that I’ve been writing them: poems addressed to objects or general categories of objects or beings (“Ode to the Hymen,” “Douche-Bag Ode”).
**Do you have a reader in mind when you write?**
I’m not sure what I have in mind while I’m writing a poem — I think I’m trying to have not much in mind! I’m trying to float above or below my mind — my own radar — and let the poem “write itself” — emerge intact from wherever in my subconscious it has been forming! A poem needs a lot of freedom, to maintain/create its own “breath” and life. I think if I were “aiming” it in some way, a poem would not have enough free will to seem alive. Having said that about the minutes of the first composition of a poem, I have to add that the thought of anyone reading a poem of mine feels like a great blessing and good fortune!
_Interview by Joy Biles_

One day when Carolyn Forché was in her twenties, a man she had never met arrived at her house with two young girls, a beat-up truck, and pages of documents concerning the history of the US government and El Salvador. This man, Leonel Gómez Vides, would alter the course of Forché’s life. In her recent memoir, _What You Have Heard Is True—_ her first published work of prose—Forché recounts the experiences that this meeting led her to witness in El Salvador in the late 1970s, just before the country was consumed by civil war.
When Leonel Gómez arrived at Forché’s door, she was living a studious life in southern California, teaching writing at a university. She had previously spent a summer in Mallorca translating the work of Nicaraguan-Salvadoran poet Claribel Alegría, whose daughter was a friend of Forché’s. Alegría had mentioned Forché’s work to Gómez, who decided he needed someone from the US to witness what was happening in El Salvador and decided to find this poet. This lead to the first of many visits Forché made to El Salvador between 1978 and 1980. While she wrote some articles about her time there, the poems in her 1981 collection, _The Country Between Us_, relate the violence and the normalization of cruelty that she witnessed in obliquely crushing, brutal language.
_What You Have Heard Is True_ recounts the people and situations Forché encountered in towns, neighborhoods, mountain villages, and rural hospitals all over the country; Gómez takes her along with him as he talks with everyone from farmers to military officers, ambassadors to informants. As the violence intensifies, she relies on excerpts pulled from her notebooks at the time to capture the imagery, sensations, and palpable tension—perhaps most apparent in what goes unsaid. Some of these images are echoed in the language of her poems on El Salvador, such as those in _The Colonel._
texts.1:
In 1993, Forché edited an anthology of poems, _Against Forgetting: Twentieth-Century Poetry of Witness_, which brought together her interests in human rights and poetry _._ The 145 works in the collection come from poets around the world who had “endured conditions of historical and social extremity during the twentieth century.” These poems were to be read within the context of a term that Forché coined in the collection’s introduction, “poetry of witness.”
Poetry of witness is not political or partisan, it is a testament to the truth. It is a witnessing of violence and a documentation of the human reaction to this violence. Forché writes in the introduction to this anthology that “these poems bear a trace of extremity within them, and they are, as such, evidence of what occurred.”
I recently spoke with Forché about the distinct ways in which journalism and poetry interact with violence and how each can be utilized to record acts against humanity—as a form of witness.
**Claire Mullen: In _What You Have Heard Is True,_ you delve into the complicated relationship between writing and personal experience. In journalism, it is antithetical to include your own experience in a story because it can indicate bias, whereas poems are often about the very personal. How do you think about the delineation between journalism and poetry in response to violence, and what was your experience with this in El Salvador?**
**Carolyn Forché:** Back then, I wrote for the _Nation_, the _Progressive_, and others, but I very happily abandoned that. I am not a journalist or a historian. I was rather free to be a literary writer and a poet and to write about my own experience because I wasn’t constricted by journalistic conventions.
There’s a frustration for journalists that they can’t speak about their experiences easily in their reporting. What I’ve noticed is that many journalists do their reporting, and then they will write a memoir or nonfiction book about their experience. For example, the great wonderful woman photographer Jean-Marie Simon who photographed throughout the War in Guatemala, and also the genocide in Guatemala, is now working on a memoir about her own experience. One of the most impressive journalists of the twentieth century, the Polish journalist Ryszard Kapuscinski, drew a line between his reporting and his own investigation of the world, as he put it, “on foot.”
texts.2:
These people have been great models for me, and it corresponds in some ways to the division between my poetry and this memoir. In the nonfiction memoir, I’m actually telling a story, and I’m trying to shape that story and structure it. I hadn’t written prose for years, and it was a challenge for me. It’s a different mind. We write from within a different consciousness when we’re writing nonfiction prose and poetry. When I’m writing poetry, I work with the associational mind; I’m not always completely conscious of what I’m doing. I would say that is less so when I was writing the nonfiction book because that was a retrieval from memory.
**CM: In the memoir, you include sections which seem to be excerpts from your notebooks from the time you were in El Salvador, and the writing verges on stream of consciousness. Some of these excerpts include sketches of ideas or imagery that are echoed in poems in _The Country Between Us._ Could you describe your writing process and how these excerpts relate to your finished poems?**
**CF:**In my adulthood as a poet, I’ve always carried small notebooks with me wherever I’ve gone. I don’t chronicle my life in them, I simply write down things as I think of them. Sometimes it’ll be a line, or a list of words, or an image that I see and I take a note of it. I’m very interested in the fact that a lot of poets that I have researched, living and dead, also kept such notebooks. It seems to be a pattern with poets.
When I was in El Salvador, I wasn’t writing poetry very much. There are only seven poems in _The Country Between Us_ that have to do with El Salvador, and most of them were written during periods when I was back in the United States. It was very intense there. There was a great deal of fear in the air, and that isn’t conducive to writing poetry. I was writing as fast as I could just to get things down before they drifted away and when I had the peace of mind or clarity to write them. They were my escape, so there are these many, many notebooks, and those passages came from them.
texts.3:
One thing that I’ve noticed is that very often when I’m writing a poem, I have the feeling that I’ve written it before. When I go back to the notebooks, I often find the vocabulary of the poem or several lines that indeed I did write before. So the seeds of the first drafts are often in the notebooks. Again, not recording my life events, but rather whatever comes from my consciousness.
**CM: Is this what you would describe as the associational thinking that you experience when writing poetry?**
**CF:**Yes. Sometimes it’ll take shape and sometimes it’s all fragmented. It’s a useful practice because it allows me to maintain the connection between the pen and the mind so that I can be surprised by what happens and make discoveries through the language itself, rather than pre-conceiving what I want to say or write. I don’t think that poetry at its best comes from preconceived message or ideas. It’s not intentional in that way.
Learning to write the memoir was a process in itself. I wrote more as a poet writes, polishing every sentence. I had a difficult time moving forward, and I also had a difficult time learning how to focus on one slice of my life. A memoir is not an autobiography, so there are many parts of life that have to be left out or just skipped over, because what you’re trying to do is tell a story that may move through time.
Also, I decided that I wanted the reader not to know more than what I knew at the time. I tried to take the reader with me on the journey that I took. I wanted to see if I could replicate it. Rather than have extensive retrospection and analysis throughout, I allowed the story to unfold without interference. Once I made that decision, I also made the discovery that inserting the excerpted passages would help me to tell the story as it happened. I could include them and it would add a dimension of a different kind of language, the kind of writing that happens under stress, and under trauma, and it’s very different, as you noticed.
**CM: Throughout the memoir, it is clear that you as a narrator are learning, you’re growing and becoming someone else. It’s fascinating that that was a deliberate choice on your part to make the reader learn along with the narrator.**
**CF:**Well, thank you. What I wanted to do was to write a transformative memoir.

Title: Sharon Olds

### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
Photo by Catherine Mauger
**Sharon Olds** was born in San Francisco and studied at Stanford University and Columbia University. When her first book was published, she was a few years shy of 40. Within a decade, she’d become the director of the Graduate Writing Program at NYU and released several highly acclaimed, best-selling collections. Her books include _Satan Says_ (1980), _The Dead and the Living_ (1984), _The Gold Cell_ (1987), _The Matter of This World_ (1987), _The Sign of Saturn_ (1991), _The Father_ (1992), _The Wellspring_ (1996), _Blood, Tin, Straw_ (1999), _The Unswept Room_ (2002), _Strike Sparks_ (2004), and _One Secret Thing_ (2008). Her poems have also appeared in more than 100 poetry anthologies.   
Olds was poet laureate of New York from 1998 to 2000. Her many honors include the T.S. Eliot Prize, the National Book Critics Circle Award, and the Pulitzer Prize. Her most recent collection, _Stag’s Leap_, came out in 2012.
**What started you writing poetry?**
I started writing poems as a child and teenager. I think what made me start was the desire to “sing,” to make up word songs, to play with words and rhymes, to tell a story.
**Your collection _Stag’s Leap_ won both the T.S Eliot Prize and the Pulitzer Prize last year. These intimate poems chronicle the dissolution of a marriage of 32 years after the husband abruptly leaves his wife for another woman. Can you speak about the title? _Stag’s Leap_ evokes such exuberance and vitality in contrast with the many painful images throughout the book.**

### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
The title poem is named after a wine, in fact after a wine label, which has a picture of a leaping deer on it. The poem is a portrait of a departing or escaping creature. I’m glad if it has vitality! I guess my hope would be that the images in the book, painful or not, would have their own vitality and give the reader pleasure.
**What was the process like assembling the poems as a whole?**
First I assembled all the poems I’d written on the subject, over 10 years, which I’d liked well enough to type up and revise. (Which was a fraction of the number I’d written on the subject.) Then I tried to narrow the group down to what I thought were the best of them, and then I looked for how they seemed to organize themselves. I did this on the dining room floor! Changing the order over and over until it seemed right.
**When people describe your work, they inevitably talk about its autobiographical aspects. In fact, _Stag’s Leap_ can be found under “Biographies and Memoirs” on Amazon, which seems unusual for a book of poetry. Do you mind being considered a distinctly autobiographical poet?**
What interests me most about the poems I read (and write) are things like the images, the music (rhyme and meter), and how the sentence and the line interconnect with each other in the poem. Over the years, I haven’t talked much about biographies and memoirs — though I love reading them; what has interested me most about poems is the art of them — what each one is doing, and how.
**You’ve said that you want a poem to be useful above all else. Can you talk about this a bit more?**
I think the arts exist because they are useful — essential to our species. I think it’s part of being human, to make art and need art. For the pleasure of it, and for whatever knowledge we get out of it. Reading each other helps us imagine each other. And empathy seems like something we are in great need of, as a species, in order to survive.
**Although your work is commonly described as free verse, you’ve mentioned that your next book will concentrate on odes. Is it liberating or particularly challenging to work in a more formal structure?**

### Welcome to **The Writer's Almanac Bookshelf**, where you'll find highlighted interviews of poets heard on the show.
I have not, over the years, tried to write in a particular form, but when I look at my poems, I see that they have been written in four-beat lines (four strong accents, however many syllables the line has), with few end-stopped lines, and a lot of enjambment (the sentence pouring over the end of one line into the next). So I see myself as a formal poet: four-beat lines, and enjambment, and internal — rather than end-stopped — rhyme being my form. (I don’t see myself as writing “free verse.”)
As for the odes I’ve been writing, they may not be odes at all — I’ve been afraid to look up _ode_ in case it’s an illusion of mind that I’ve been writing them: poems addressed to objects or general categories of objects or beings (“Ode to the Hymen,” “Douche-Bag Ode”).
**Do you have a reader in mind when you write?**
I’m not sure what I have in mind while I’m writing a poem — I think I’m trying to have not much in mind! I’m trying to float above or below my mind — my own radar — and let the poem “write itself” — emerge intact from wherever in my subconscious it has been forming! A poem needs a lot of freedom, to maintain/create its own “breath” and life. I think if I were “aiming” it in some way, a poem would not have enough free will to seem alive. Having said that about the minutes of the first composition of a poem, I have to add that the thought of anyone reading a poem of mine feels like a great blessing and good fortune!
_Interview by Joy Biles_

Title: “Poetry has great work to do”: An Interview with Carolyn Forché
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
One day when Carolyn Forché was in her twenties, a man she had never met arrived at her house with two young girls, a beat-up truck, and pages of documents concerning the history of the US government and El Salvador. This man, Leonel Gómez Vides, would alter the course of Forché’s life. In her recent memoir, _What You Have Heard Is True—_ her first published work of prose—Forché recounts the experiences that this meeting led her to witness in El Salvador in the late 1970s, just before the country was consumed by civil war.
When Leonel Gómez arrived at Forché’s door, she was living a studious life in southern California, teaching writing at a university. She had previously spent a summer in Mallorca translating the work of Nicaraguan-Salvadoran poet Claribel Alegría, whose daughter was a friend of Forché’s. Alegría had mentioned Forché’s work to Gómez, who decided he needed someone from the US to witness what was happening in El Salvador and decided to find this poet. This lead to the first of many visits Forché made to El Salvador between 1978 and 1980. While she wrote some articles about her time there, the poems in her 1981 collection, _The Country Between Us_, relate the violence and the normalization of cruelty that she witnessed in obliquely crushing, brutal language.
_What You Have Heard Is True_ recounts the people and situations Forché encountered in towns, neighborhoods, mountain villages, and rural hospitals all over the country; Gómez takes her along with him as he talks with everyone from farmers to military officers, ambassadors to informants. As the violence intensifies, she relies on excerpts pulled from her notebooks at the time to capture the imagery, sensations, and palpable tension—perhaps most apparent in what goes unsaid. Some of these images are echoed in the language of her poems on El Salvador, such as those in _The Colonel._

In 1993, Forché edited an anthology of poems, _Against Forgetting: Twentieth-Century Poetry of Witness_, which brought together her interests in human rights and poetry _._ The 145 works in the collection come from poets around the world who had “endured conditions of historical and social extremity during the twentieth century.” These poems were to be read within the context of a term that Forché coined in the collection’s introduction, “poetry of witness.”
Poetry of witness is not political or partisan, it is a testament to the truth. It is a witnessing of violence and a documentation of the human reaction to this violence. Forché writes in the introduction to this anthology that “these poems bear a trace of extremity within them, and they are, as such, evidence of what occurred.”
I recently spoke with Forché about the distinct ways in which journalism and poetry interact with violence and how each can be utilized to record acts against humanity—as a form of witness.
**Claire Mullen: In _What You Have Heard Is True,_ you delve into the complicated relationship between writing and personal experience. In journalism, it is antithetical to include your own experience in a story because it can indicate bias, whereas poems are often about the very personal. How do you think about the delineation between journalism and poetry in response to violence, and what was your experience with this in El Salvador?**
**Carolyn Forché:** Back then, I wrote for the _Nation_, the _Progressive_, and others, but I very happily abandoned that. I am not a journalist or a historian. I was rather free to be a literary writer and a poet and to write about my own experience because I wasn’t constricted by journalistic conventions.
There’s a frustration for journalists that they can’t speak about their experiences easily in their reporting. What I’ve noticed is that many journalists do their reporting, and then they will write a memoir or nonfiction book about their experience. For example, the great wonderful woman photographer Jean-Marie Simon who photographed throughout the War in Guatemala, and also the genocide in Guatemala, is now working on a memoir about her own experience. One of the most impressive journalists of the twentieth century, the Polish journalist Ryszard Kapuscinski, drew a line between his reporting and his own investigation of the world, as he put it, “on foot.”

These people have been great models for me, and it corresponds in some ways to the division between my poetry and this memoir. In the nonfiction memoir, I’m actually telling a story, and I’m trying to shape that story and structure it. I hadn’t written prose for years, and it was a challenge for me. It’s a different mind. We write from within a different consciousness when we’re writing nonfiction prose and poetry. When I’m writing poetry, I work with the associational mind; I’m not always completely conscious of what I’m doing. I would say that is less so when I was writing the nonfiction book because that was a retrieval from memory.
**CM: In the memoir, you include sections which seem to be excerpts from your notebooks from the time you were in El Salvador, and the writing verges on stream of consciousness. Some of these excerpts include sketches of ideas or imagery that are echoed in poems in _The Country Between Us._ Could you describe your writing process and how these excerpts relate to your finished poems?**
**CF:**In my adulthood as a poet, I’ve always carried small notebooks with me wherever I’ve gone. I don’t chronicle my life in them, I simply write down things as I think of them. Sometimes it’ll be a line, or a list of words, or an image that I see and I take a note of it. I’m very interested in the fact that a lot of poets that I have researched, living and dead, also kept such notebooks. It seems to be a pattern with poets.
When I was in El Salvador, I wasn’t writing poetry very much. There are only seven poems in _The Country Between Us_ that have to do with El Salvador, and most of them were written during periods when I was back in the United States. It was very intense there. There was a great deal of fear in the air, and that isn’t conducive to writing poetry. I was writing as fast as I could just to get things down before they drifted away and when I had the peace of mind or clarity to write them. They were my escape, so there are these many, many notebooks, and those passages came from them.

One thing that I’ve noticed is that very often when I’m writing a poem, I have the feeling that I’ve written it before. When I go back to the notebooks, I often find the vocabulary of the poem or several lines that indeed I did write before. So the seeds of the first drafts are often in the notebooks. Again, not recording my life events, but rather whatever comes from my consciousness.
**CM: Is this what you would describe as the associational thinking that you experience when writing poetry?**
**CF:**Yes. Sometimes it’ll take shape and sometimes it’s all fragmented. It’s a useful practice because it allows me to maintain the connection between the pen and the mind so that I can be surprised by what happens and make discoveries through the language itself, rather than pre-conceiving what I want to say or write. I don’t think that poetry at its best comes from preconceived message or ideas. It’s not intentional in that way.
Learning to write the memoir was a process in itself. I wrote more as a poet writes, polishing every sentence. I had a difficult time moving forward, and I also had a difficult time learning how to focus on one slice of my life. A memoir is not an autobiography, so there are many parts of life that have to be left out or just skipped over, because what you’re trying to do is tell a story that may move through time.
Also, I decided that I wanted the reader not to know more than what I knew at the time. I tried to take the reader with me on the journey that I took. I wanted to see if I could replicate it. Rather than have extensive retrospection and analysis throughout, I allowed the story to unfold without interference. Once I made that decision, I also made the discovery that inserting the excerpted passages would help me to tell the story as it happened. I could include them and it would add a dimension of a different kind of language, the kind of writing that happens under stress, and under trauma, and it’s very different, as you noticed.
**CM: Throughout the memoir, it is clear that you as a narrator are learning, you’re growing and becoming someone else. It’s fascinating that that was a deliberate choice on your part to make the reader learn along with the narrator.**
**CF:**Well, thank you. What I wanted to do was to write a transformative memoir.

Source: https://www.chicagotribune.com/1986/05/23/myth-finally-gives-way-to-emilys-poetry/
Title: MYTH FINALLY GIVES WAY TO EMILY`S POETRY
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
They carried her in a white shroud out the back door of her father`s house, across fields of buttercups and daisies, to a cemetery on the edge of town. At the age of 55, the author of only 10 published poems, Emily Dickinson had died utterly unknown.
One hundred springs later, it is finals week at Amherst College, and young women in cotton skirts and bare feet come to sit with their backs to the cold granite in West Cemetery, reading from the thick volume of 1,775 poems that Emily Dickinson had placed in a drawer in her room before her death on May 15, 1886.
To the Dickinson house on the Main Street come enthusiasts from around the world, including an enraptured group of Japanese who visited a week ago. They climb the stairs, walk down the hallway and turn right into the corner bedroom where Dickinson long hid from the world, her pen scratching, scratching at a table by the window.
And they marvel, as did present-day poet Adrienne Rich, that ”here in this white-curtained, high-ceilinged room, a red-haired woman with hazel eyes and a contralto voice wrote poems about volcanos, deserts, eternity, suicide, physical passion, wild beasts, rape, power, madness, separation, the daemon, the grave.”
Today, after a decade of fresh critical study, including her adoption as a ”foremother” by feminist poets, Emily Dickinson has ascended to the pinnacle of American literature.
With Walt Whitman–the contemporary of whom she said, ”I never read his book, but was told that he was disgraceful”–she is almost universally ranked as one of America`s two poetic geniuses of the 19th Century and, almost as certainly, as one of the greatest who ever wrote in English.
Thus, the centennial of her death has evolved into a major literary event, drawing scholars and fans to poetry readings and celebrations by Amherst, the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington, the University of North Carolina, the University of California and other institutions. The Folger also has undertaken an Emily Dickinson centennial exhibition, which will run through June.
Daniel Lombardo, curator of special collections at the Amherst town library, where a number of Dickinson manuscripts are housed, has studied the pilgrims who come and go.

”There`s a kind of Emily Dickinson worship going on,” he said. ”People approach Amherst as if it were some kind of holy place. It`s funny. You don`t get the same breed of people who come for Robert Frost (who also lived in Amherst and taught for many years at the college). There`s not the magnetism that Emily has for people.
”They misidentify with Emily by thinking she escaped from the world. People think, `Wouldn`t it be nice to live in the 19th Century, in this beautiful house, in this lovely little college town?` People who may be a little eccentric end up dressing like her and trying to write poetry like her.”
This kind of identification isn`t hard to understand for another reason, as well.
So reclusive in her later years that she rarely went out and often ran from visitors, Dickinson spoke to the reader with an intimacy that can be stunning, almost embarrassing–about passion, yes, but mostly about the tremors of the soul.
”My own words,” she said, ”so chill and burn me.”
The lore and myth of Emily Dickinson–the spinster in the paisley shawl peeking at the world from behind white curtains; the maid with the hoe in the garden; the cookie-baker lowering a basket of ginger snaps on a string to children in the neighborhood–has for too long eclipsed the poetry of Emily Dickinson.
Add to this myth a puritanical father, an aloof and incomprehending mother and the poet`s own hints of a crushed and mysterious love affair–and you have the makings of a cult.
At times, some of the most obsessed of admirers seem hardly to have read her. But at least they kept her fame alive during all the years when critics were patronizing her.
Her literary mentor, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, called her ”my eccentric poetess” and confessed that he did not understand her. ”You only enshroud yourself in this fiery mist,” he complained in a letter, ”and I cannot reach you.”
The handful of Dickinson poems that saw print in her lifetime were published anonymously. The first batch with her name on them came out in 1890, four years after her death. But those reflected only part of Dickinson`s work. They tended to be the poems that dealt with the then-accepted women`s themes of nature and beauty.

Her poetry on the great themes of God, death and immortality trickled out over decades. It wasn`t until 1955, nearly three-quarters of a century after her death, that ”The Complete Poems of Emily Dickinson,” edited by Harvard scholar Thomas H. Johnson, was published.
Then it took years more for a generation of critics and scholars steeped in Dickinson to come to the fore.
Now, at last, the poetry may be triumphing over the myth.
Katharine Zadravec, director of the recent Emily Dickinson conference at the Folger Shakespeare Library, put it this way: ”People get caught up in:
Was she an erotic? Was she a psychotic? A recluse? A nun? A mystic? Why did she hide away? Why did she wear white? Why didn`t she publish?. That`s not the point. The point is, she was a great writer of great poetry.”
”Emily Dickinson`s life, in a sense almost unique among poets, was her work,” wrote Richard B. Sewall, a retired Yale professor whose massive 1980 biography helped reshape her image.
Critic Alfred Kazin, a participant in the Washington conference, said in an interview recently that her poems make up ”the most extraordinary personal novel ever written.”
Both Sewall and Kazin warned against reading too much from the poems. Readers, they say, who look for evidence of sexual affairs–even, as some have suggested, a homosexual affair–will make a mistake: The poet is a great deceiver.
Little is known about her life. She may, indeed, have had a lover; Sewall and Kazin think not. But in the usual sense–Where did she go? What did she do? What did she accomplish?–there is little to know about Emily Dickinson.
She was the middle of three children in a prominent family, descended from generations of clergymen and educators, the first of whom arrived in New England in 1630, only 10 years after the Pilgrims.
The town of Amherst was a center of learning, despite its remote location in the middle of Massachusetts, and most of the literati who came to Amherst visited the Dickinsons` handsome brick house, with its white Grecian pillars and cupola.

The poet`s father, Edward Dickinson, was domineering, albeit in a way that was typical of the era. He believed in education, in frugality and in rigorous daily battle with Satan. A congressman for a time, he wrote letters home to his children in which he exhorted them to proper conduct but neglected to say he loved them. The Freudians have had great fun with him.
The mother, too. Dr. John Cody, a Kansas psychiatrist with a devotion to Dickinson, portrays Emily Norcross Dickinson as a compulsive housekeeper, intellectually sluggish in a brilliant household, who never gave her daughter the love she needed. She was also, Cody has concluded, a hypochondriac.
The young Emily was sent off to Mt. Holyoke Female Seminary for a proper New England education. There is a picture of her at school; it is the only one extant.
She is 16. Her hair is parted severely down the middle and pinned tightly behind her head. She is thin and awkward-looking in the manner of an adolescent. Her lips are pursed. She is plain, but not unattractive.
As she grew older, she wrote more and more poetry; and as she wrote more and more poetry, she gradually began to recede from the life of Amherst. By the time she was in her 30s, she was effectively a stay-at-home, working, working in that lovely corner room at the top of the stairs.
Visitors there are wont to commune with spirits. Elizabeth DeBevoise, the cultured woman who occupies the rest of the house, which is owned by Amherst College, said that she herself was no ”mystic.” But she understands why others may be.
”No other house is so closely associated with anyone like Emily Dickinson–if there is anyone like Emily Dickinson,” she said. ”It was where she was born, she lived all but 15 years . . . here, she did her work here and she died here.”
It has long been debated whether Emily Dickinson wished to publish or not. Her few experiences with the literary world were not good ones. Her poems were edited; she was advised to get in step.
Scholars now generally believe that she was more decisive, more calculating than her myth would indicate. She probably made a conscious decision not to publish, thus enabling herself to write what she wished and to live the life of the mind she desired.

Essays on Dickinson were published several years ago in a book titled
”Shakespeare`s Sisters: Feminist Essays on Women Poets.” The title was taken from Virginia Woolf, who wrote that ”if Shakespeare had had a greatly gifted sister . . . who had tried to use her gift for poetry,” she surely would have gone mad; for women poets had always been regarded as oddities and freaks.
But Maxine Kumin, another New England poet, said in an interview that it seems likely that Emily Dickinson ”was not reclusive out of agoraphobia, but out of self-preservation.”
For her, that spare upper room was not confinement. It was freedom.

a style influenced by Gabriel Fauré and Henri Duparc; 38 one is dedicated to Fauré and
another to Hahn ’s close friend Marcel Proust. Their mood is predominantly gentle and
subdued, with frequent markings such as “calme,” “tendre,” “modéré” and “sérieux.”
Hahn’s cycle has fared well on recordings: there are complete versions by Ian Bostridge
and Stephen Var coe 39 and by Bruno Laplante. 40
Almost all musical settings of Horace prior to the twentieth century, whether
based on the original Latin or a translation, aim at an effect that can be described as
contemporary: they adapt Horace to the musical style of the period, whether that style is
that of a sixteenth -century polyphonic motet or a nineteenth -century German
Männerchor . In the twentieth century, by contrast, a number of composers have chosen to
set Horace’s Latin in conscious imitation of an earlier style, as a way of highlighting its
otherness. (A similar use of Latin for its distancing effect can be seen in Stravinsky’s
Oedipus Rex and in Carl Orff’s cantatas based on Catullus and the medieval Carmina
Burana .) One exemplar of this deliberately archaizing approach is the American
composer Randall Thompson, best known for his choral writing; his Alleluia (1940) is
among the most often -performed choral works of the century. 41 Thompson cultivated a
lifelong interest in the musical styles of earlier periods, esp ecially sixteenth -century
polyphony; in an informal set of reflections composed near the end of his life he wrote
“my heart still leaps up when I see a cantus firmus.” 42 Among his earliest published 14
compositions are settings of five odes of Horace, written in 1924 -25 during his tenure of
a Rome Prize at the American Academy. 43 They show the influence of Thompson’s

# Share Your Story
mentor Gian Francesco Malipiero, who at the time was immersing himself in the music
of Monteverdi and his contemporaries. Almost thirty years later , in 1953, as a tribute to
his Harvard teacher and colleague Archibald T. Davison on his retirement, Thompson
returned to the Odes and composed a four -voice setting in the style of Palestrina of the
final stanza (lines 17 -20) of Odes 1.13:
Felices ter et amplius
quos inrupta tenet copula nec malis
divulsus querimoniis
suprema citius solvet amor die .
(Three times happy they, and more,
who are held in an unbroken bond,
whose love, divided by no bitter quarrels,
will not loose them before their last day.) 44
For Thompson, the text must have seemed appropriate as a way to express his affection
for the work’s dedicatee; 45 he also recalled that he chose it because it appeared as an
inscription on one of the gates leading into Harvard Yard. 46 In its original Horatia n
context, though, the stanza is considerably more problematic, and interesting. In the four
stanzas that precede it, Horace details his jealous reactions when he hears Lydia (a former
lover?) praising her boyfriend Telephus. His rage and despair are descr ibed in terms that
strongly suggest parody of conventional love poetry. The swerve into apparent high 15
seriousness in the closing lines thus presents the reader with a challenge of interpretation:
is Horace setting an ideal vision of love against a foolishl y romantic version, is he
showing Lydia a kind of love she has no chance of enjoying with Telephus, or is he
ruefully reflecting on what he himself had failed to achieve in his relationship with her? 47
This complexity disappears entirely when the final stan za is detached from its setting and
read (or sung) in isolation. 48
Even this highly selective discussion makes it clear that Horatian lyric has
appealed to a wide range of composers over a long span of time. But surveying how the
odes have been set also ma kes us more aware of the difficulties they pose for musical
treatment. The verbal density of Horace’s writing is one obstacle; another is the

# Share Your Story
awkwardness of his preferred line -lengths for modern musical styles. Many odes are too
long to be comfortably set, especially if the musical handling is to have any complexity
or richness. But perhaps the greatest challenge is posed by the variety of tone and content
that Horace often encompasses within a single ode, a variety made all the more striking
by the repetit ion of the same metrical patterns throughout a poem. One of Horace’s best
modern critics has written that “to cover ground is a merit in a poet,” 49 but music with a
repeating stanzaic base does not readily express such differences of mood within a
piece. 50 Those features, the last in particular, help to explain why so many settings have
been made of parts of odes or even of individual stanzas, in which the musical treatment
could evoke a single emotional mood, even if one not consistent with the Horatian text as
a whole. 51 In this as in other respects, Horace’s lyric poetry, which appears so direct and
approachable, turns out to be stubbornly elusive. 16
Musicians are not the only readers of Horace who have plucked lines and stanzas
out of their context in orde r to give them a more straightforward meaning. The same
impulse lies behind the creation of anthologies of poetic excerpts, or florilegia , of which
numerous examples survive from the Middle Ages and the early modern period. As it
happens, both Odes 1.13.17 -20 ( Felices ter ) and 1.22.1 -8 ( Integer vitae ) appear in some
manuscripts of the most widely circulated medieval anthology of excerpts from classical
poetry, known as the Florilegium Gallicum ; the former passage is listed under the
heading De concordia con iugali (“On marital harmony”) and the latter is headed Que
sunt commoda innocentie ad amicum (“The advantages of innocence, to a friend”). 52
Perhaps because of the difficulties that Horace’s Latin lyrics pose for musical
setting, a closer approach in musi c to the spirit of the Odes can sometimes be achieved by
a less immediate relationship to their text. That is to say, the Horatian ethos may be better
reflected in musical settings of texts that are either inspired by Horace or compatible with

poems (none longer than sixteen lines), in keeping with Thompson’s precept for choosing
a text for musical treatment: “choose a good text and not t oo long a text” (Thompson
(1980) 11). Performances of 1.23, 1.30 , and 3.13 are included in “Rome’s Golden Poets.”

can say ‘I have lived’”); for the music see Deutsch (1959) 33. Haydn’s tombstone bears a

> 52
See Burton (1983) 278 -9. The role of florilegia in guiding composers to isolated
passages of Horace was acutely suggested by Philip Barnes in his notes to the CD
“Rome’s Golden Poets.” For example, a florilegium is very probably the source of the
single hexameter principibus placuisse viris non ultima laus est (“to have pleased the

couplet: summa Deo laus est qui placuisse studet (“the highest praise belongs to the one
who strives to please God”).

Nearly 400 musical settings of poems by Housman are listed by Gooch and Thatcher
(1976); they include thirty -five separate settin gs each of “Loveliest of trees, the cherry
now” and “When I was one -and -twenty.” There is apparently a more recent catalog by
Bill Lewis that lists almost 500 settings (referred to by Venables (2008) 72, 74), but I
have not yet been able to locate it. 35

Wh en Vaughan Williams dropped the two stanzas of “Is my team ploughing” referring
to football, the poet was not pleased. He wrote his publisher, Grant Richards, “I am told
that composers in some cases have mutilated my poems, — that Vaughan Williams cut

bars out of his music).” See Burnett (2007) 1.458. Housman even took offense when

thought he wa s therefore entitled to print the texts of the poems in a concert program. See

2006, “Ms. Panetti said that the title was taken from a Theodore Roethke poem in which
the poet warns us that time, the instant, is passing so we had best make the most of it.” 36
Tommasini went on to write th at “she has put the poet's advice to good use in this
eventful, intense yet impressively economical 13 -minute, three -movement work.” The

locate the phrase itself in Roethke’s work, although I have noted two occurrences of “the
instant ages” (“but now the instant ages” in “Give way, ye gates” and “the instant ages on
the living eye” in “Infirmity”). A query to the composer was not answered.
